Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes

Robert Fonod Email: robert.fonod@ieee.org Affiliation: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Urban Transport Systems Laboratory (LUTS), Station 18, CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Corresponding author: Corresponding author.    Nikolas Geroliminis Affiliation: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Urban Transport Systems Laboratory (LUTS), Station 18, CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract

Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group’s displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.00620.0062, and masking costs less than 0.0050.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 2828 of 304304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 66 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px18.8\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

Keywords:
UAV video stabilization , image registration , homography estimation , feature matching , oriented bounding box , traffic monitoring

1 Introduction

Reference-frame stabilization is the registration model used when object positions must stay consistent over a long hover, during which wind keeps shifting and rotating the view: every frame is aligned directly onto one fixed reference frame, so that error does not accumulate and a position measured in frame kk is comparable with one measured minutes earlier. Trajectory extraction from high-altitude UAV (UAV) video is the application studied here, and traffic monitoring supplies the footage, but the requirement is shared by any analysis that compares moving objects across time in image or map coordinates, such as river surface velocimetry (Ljubičić et al., 2021a). The estimate is a homography, and the pipeline that produces it (feature detector, descriptor, matcher, robust estimator, and, where objects are annotated, a masking strategy that withholds them from feature detection) is assembled from components each of which has been benchmarked extensively (Jin et al., 2021a; Efe et al., 2021a; Barath et al., 2023a).

Those benchmarks evaluate correspondence accuracy on scenes without independently moving content: planar surfaces, landmark facades, building walls. The only source of disagreement between their two views is the camera. A hovering drone over a busy intersection presents the opposite case. The camera barely moves, and dozens of objects in the frame move without it, many of them together: a platoon released by a green light translates as a unit, and every vehicle in it supplies correspondences that agree with one another under a single transform, the one describing their motion. If those correspondences win the consensus, the robust estimator does not fail. It solves the problem it was posed, returning a homography that is internally consistent and well supported but describes the vehicles rather than the road (Fig. 1).

We call this failure consensus capture, and it has a consequence for evaluation before it has one for method design. Inlier count, inlier ratio, and reprojection error measure the self-consistency of a fit, and a coherently moving foreground is self-consistent by construction. Where it wins, these quantities are no longer merely weak proxies for accuracy, as they are already known to be on static scenes (Jin et al., 2021a; Barath et al., 2023a); they become anti-informative, because the moving-object consensus can be the cleaner of the two available fits. An evaluation that reads them cannot detect capture. What is needed scores the alignment of the static world directly, makes a moving-object consensus observable, and relates it to how much of the frame moves and how coherently. To our knowledge no matching or registration benchmark provides this: none combines independently moving content with reference geometry (Section 2), so a risk flagged for airborne video (Kirchhof & Stilla, 2006a) has gone unmeasured.

Capture matters most where trajectories are used one at a time. Macroscopic quantities such as flow and density average a transient offset away, but microscopic analyses read individual trajectories and their derivatives: car following, lane changes (Kim et al., 2026a), per-vehicle noise emission (Espadaler-Clapés et al., 2023a), and surrogate safety measures such as time-to-collision, post-encroachment time and the deceleration rate to avoid a crash (Abdel-Aty et al., 2023a; Espadaler-Clapés et al., 2025a), which drone trajectory datasets now provide or are built to support (Zheng et al., 2024a; Fonod et al., 2025b). Under reference-frame registration each frame is registered on its own, so nothing ties a captured estimate to those of neighboring frames: its error follows the group’s motion and is present only while the group holds the consensus. Speeds and accelerations are differences of positions over fractions of a second, so an error that varies from frame to frame in this way is amplified in them (Punzo et al., 2011a). The accuracy these datasets aim for is correspondingly tight: the inD dataset requires a positioning error below 0.1 m0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{m} (Bock et al., 2020a), under two pixels at the GSD (GSD) of the footage studied here (Section 3), whereas the captured estimates of Section 7.3 have a median corner error of 18.8 px18.8\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, about a meter on the ground, against the reference estimator. Since the estimates pulled toward the group keep typical inlier statistics, a pipeline captured on a few frames passes their error, unflagged, to every trajectory in those frames. Several of these datasets are also recorded lower than the 140 m to 150 m140\text{\,}\mathrm{m}150\text{\,}\mathrm{m} studied here: inD from up to 100 m100\text{\,}\mathrm{m} at about 4 cm4\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} per pixel (Bock et al., 2020a) and the intersections of CitySim from 120 m120\text{\,}\mathrm{m} (Zheng et al., 2024a); a view that covers less ground can give a vehicle group of the same size a larger share of the frame and of its features.

We provide such an evaluation in two parts. Part I is a static protocol under exactly known homographies and photometric degradation, on 4K frames from a multi-drone experiment over Songdo, South Korea: one from each of the 2929 viewpoints from which its ten drones recorded 2020 intersections. It establishes what each pipeline can do when nothing moves and which of its settings matter, extending the campaign of Fonod et al. (2025b) with paired trials, per-pipeline tuning on a site-disjoint split, and a matched resolution and feature budget. Part II is a dynamic protocol on nine hovers over busy intersections, each registered onto a reference frame selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control that separates the removal of moving objects from the removal of texture. It runs every pipeline at an offline and a real-time point of Part I’s budget grid. Real footage has no true homography, so Part II measures background alignment outside the annotated objects, the position error a trajectory inherits, the direction of the error relative to the dominant motion, and the share of a moving group’s displacement an estimate follows, which measures capture where it happens. Its pseudo-ground-truth reference estimator is audited against manually annotated GCP (image positions of static ground points, not surveyed coordinates), which also score every candidate directly, so that the masking comparison does not depend on the reference estimator’s own masking. Masking with HBB and OBB is a controlled axis throughout, since the shape of a mask could matter in either direction (Section 5).

On hovers over Songdo intersections, the measurement finds capture. At the real-time budget, unmasked ORB is captured in all five cases that present a coherently moving group, the four with much moving foreground and the stationary control, on 2828 of the 304304 pairs that carry one, though 2222 of them in a single case. The 1717 within the first second are pulls toward the group; 1010 of the 1111 beyond it are breakdowns of the estimate, which unmasked ORB also shows with no group in view. At the offline budget capture is rarer (unmasked ORB, 66 pairs in two cases). Estimates pulled toward a group cannot be told apart by their inlier statistics: their inlier counts and ratios match those of the same pipeline at the nearest offsets of the same case, at both budgets. Masking removes capture for every pipeline at both budgets while leaving the leading pipelines, SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE, where they were; for real-time ORB, whose feature budget it also returns to the ground, the captured pairs can account for at most a quarter of the gain. HBB and OBB do not differ at these densities and orientations, where the two geometries withhold nearly the same pixels. Averaged over all nine cases, four of which never present a moving group, the masking benefit is either not significant or smaller than the repeatability of the GCP (Section 7.5). The conclusions are bounded by the moving share of these cases; the protocol is not, and it applies unchanged to footage from lower altitude or over denser traffic, where that share is larger.

1.1 Contributions

  1. 1.

    A benchmark for the complete registration pipeline of reference-based UAV stabilization in dynamic urban scenes: a static protocol under exactly known homographies (Section 6) and a dynamic protocol on real hovering-drone footage at an offline and a real-time compute budget (Section 7). It covers the pipelines a deployed stabilization library exposes, as a measurement of that system rather than a leaderboard of state-of-the-art matchers (Section 3.2).

  2. 2.

    An evaluation methodology for dynamic scenes, where self-consistency statistics are unreliable: background-alignment measures that need no ground-truth homography, object-level errors that bound the position error a trajectory inherits, two measures that make consensus capture observable (the direction of the error and the share of a moving group’s displacement an estimate follows), and a GCP audit that measures the error of the pseudo-ground truth and supplies an independent comparison (Section 4), under a pre-specified analysis plan (Section 4.9).

  3. 3.

    A case-selection procedure that measures from the video alone how much of the foreground moves, how coherently, and when, and chooses the cases and their reference frames to span these conditions, under which capture can arise; its measurements are validated against published vehicle trajectories (Section 7.1).

  4. 4.

    A measurement of consensus capture and of object-aware masking on real footage: at the real-time budget unmasked ORB is captured in every case that presents a coherent group, its pull toward the group is invisible to inlier statistics, and capture disappears under masking at detection (Sections 7.3 and 7.5).

  5. 5.

    The public release of the benchmark implementation (Fonod, 2026f) and of its data (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026b) (annotated frames, cases, GCP and every campaign’s results), from which every benchmark number is regenerated by a command. Also released are hbb2obb (Fonod, 2026e), the SAM-assisted conversion of HBB to OBB that makes OBB masks available at benchmark scale, and Songdo Vision OBB (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026c), the OBB version of Songdo Vision (Fonod et al., 2026a), together with the human-verified oriented reference against which the conversion is validated (Sections 5.1 and E).

2 Related work

Local features and matching

Correspondence estimation has been surveyed repeatedly as it moved from hand-crafted operators to learned ones (Ma et al., 2021a). The pipelines benchmarked here span three generations of that work. Hand-crafted detectors and descriptors, from SIFT (Lowe, 2004a) and its RootSIFT normalization (Arandjelović & Zisserman, 2012a) to the binary ORB (Rublee et al., 2011a) and BRISK (Leutenegger et al., 2011a) and the nonlinear scale spaces of KAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2012a) and AKAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2013a), remain the default in deployed stabilization pipelines, because they need no training data, no accelerator, and no assumption about the imagery. Learned detectors and descriptors replace one or both stages with a network trained for repeatability and matchability, among them SuperPoint (DeTone et al., 2018a), DISK (Tyszkiewicz et al., 2020a), DeDoDe (Edstedt et al., 2024b), Key.Net (Barroso-Laguna et al., 2019a) and XFeat (Potje et al., 2024a); learned matchers such as LightGlue (Lindenberger et al., 2023a) replace the nearest-neighbor search and its ratio test with attention over the two keypoint sets; and detector-free methods such as LoFTR (Sun et al., 2021a) drop keypoints and match dense features directly. Dense matchers such as RoMa (Edstedt et al., 2024c) go further and estimate a warp and its certainty for every pixel, from which correspondences are sampled. A stabilization pipeline is chosen as a whole and its components interact (a matcher accepts only certain descriptors, a detector-free method has no keypoint budget), so the comparison of Section 6.2 spans all three. Two properties of this literature shape the protocol. Orientation estimation is not universal, so several learned models are effectively upright, which is why rotation is swept, as Tareen & Saleem (2018a) sweep it for the classical detectors, which they find unequally invariant to it; and the input resolution of a learned model is a memory bound rather than a free choice, which is why the compute budget is an axis of the benchmark.

Direct homography regression

A parallel line of work regresses the transform from an image pair (DeTone et al., 2016a). Zhang et al. (2020a) observe that a loss computed uniformly over the image cannot keep moving or non-planar objects from contributing to it, and learn a content mask that rejects those regions: the problem measured here, approached by learning what to ignore instead of by annotating it. These methods lie outside the feature-based family deployed in the trajectory extraction systems of Section 2.

Robust estimation and dominant structure

RANSAC (Fischler & Bolles, 1981a) and its modern variants (Barath et al., 2020a; Barath & Matas, 2018a) make a homography recoverable from contaminated correspondences. That a coherent structure of outliers can capture the consensus is known (Stewart, 1997a), and Chum et al. (2005a) detect a dominant plane inside the estimator; Section 4.1 explains why that defense does not transfer to a coherently moving group. Filters that prune matches before the estimator rest on a similar vote: Jiang & Jiang (2018a) keep matches whose motion agrees in direction and length, Zhou et al. (2024a) build local motion consensus into a learned matcher, and the motions of a coherently moving group agree as well.

Scenes with more than one structure

Multi-model fitting accepts that a scene may contain several coherent structures and recovers them jointly, by clustering correspondences (Toldo & Fusiello, 2008a; Wong et al., 2011a) or by fitting instances progressively inside the robust estimator (Barath & Matas, 2019a). Vehicles crossing an intersection are such a second structure, and AdelaideRMF (Wong et al., 2011a) does contain independently moving content. These methods are evaluated by how well correspondences are partitioned among structures, not by the accuracy of one recovered transform, and AdelaideRMF supplies no reference homography for the background. Recovering several homographies also leaves open which one describes the ground, which correspondence counts cannot decide when the moving structure is the larger. Multi-model fitting is a remedy that changes the estimator; what is missing first is a measurement of the failure under the estimators actually deployed.

Benchmarks for matching and homography estimation

Comparative studies of classical detectors and descriptors (Tareen & Saleem, 2018a) and HPatches (Balntas et al., 2017a) established the vocabulary this field still uses, and Schonberger et al. (2017a) set the pattern of judging hand-crafted and learned features on a common downstream task. Three benchmarks set the methodological standard we adopt. Jin et al. (2021a) argue that local features must be judged by a downstream task rather than by intermediate proxies, and show that carefully tuned classical pipelines remain competitive with learned ones, a conclusion Efe et al. (2021a) reach on HPatches by optimizing a single parameter; Barath et al. (2023a) contribute a large-scale homography benchmark with an explicit tuning-and-test protocol. Their shared lesson is that a comparison is only as meaningful as the care taken to place every method on equal footing (Section 4.7). None of them measures registration accuracy on a scene whose content moves independently of the camera (Table 1), because their reference geometry, SfM (SfM) or manually labeled correspondences on static structure, must exclude independently moving objects to work at all. Registration benchmarks that do model change place it between acquisitions (Sun et al., 2025a). Pseudo-ground truth has a further cost: Brachmann et al. (2021a) show that the algorithm generating it can reorder the methods evaluated against it, which is why the reference estimator of Part II is audited against GCP (Section 4.8).

Suppressing moving objects before geometry is estimated

Excluding independently moving content before a geometric model is fitted is established practice in dynamic SLAM (SLAM). DynaSLAM (Bescos et al., 2018a) and DS-SLAM (Yu et al., 2018a) segment likely-moving classes and withhold those regions from tracking and mapping. Both report that suppression keeps the estimate usable in populated scenes; what is missing is a measurement. Those systems are evaluated end to end, by trajectory error on indoor sequences with a handful of walking people or on driving sequences, which does not say how much of the frame the objects may cover before the consensus shifts to them, which box geometry is worth its cost, or what the failure looks like without suppression. A hovering drone over an intersection is the opposite regime: a nearly static camera and dozens of vehicles moving in coherent streams. Isolating the effect needs the masking strategy varied as a controlled axis while everything else is held fixed (Section 7.5), and a metric that does not read the objects themselves (Section 4.3).

Video stabilization as a different objective

Stabilization also names work whose goal is a pleasant camera path rather than a fixed frame of reference: smoothing the path under geometric constraints (Grundmann et al., 2011a), over a mesh of local homographies (Liu et al., 2013a), or by learning the warp (Yu & Ramamoorthi, 2020a). Its measures (cropping ratio, distortion, a frequency-domain stability score) follow from a perceptual objective, and none asks where a pixel actually is. A smoothed path may drift from any particular frame, which is inadmissible when object positions are compared across a recording, and a mesh of local warps can absorb independent object motion instead of rejecting it. Moving objects enter this literature as a threat to the global motion estimate, met by adaptive RANSAC (Choi et al., 2009a), clustered motion vectors (Wu et al., 2021a) or foreground trajectories (Zhao & Ling, 2019a), and scored by the similarity of the output frames, not against reference geometry.

Registration and stabilization of aerial video

Registering airborne video to a fixed reference is long established in photogrammetry (Kumar et al., 2001a). The remote sensing literature on image registration concentrates on matching across modalities, sensors and acquisition times (Geng et al., 2025a), with structural or phase-congruency descriptors built to be insensitive to radiometric change (Ye et al., 2017a; Li et al., 2020a) and networks trained on large multimodal datasets (Wu et al., 2026a), so transient content is a nuisance to be removed rather than a property to be measured.

Moving traffic in airborne registration

Vehicle measurement from the air rests on this registration (Reinartz et al., 2006a; Karimi et al., 2006a), and moving traffic is a recognized hazard to it. Kirchhof & Stilla (2006a) warn that many objects moving in the same direction, as on dense roads, can survive RANSAC and bias the homography, and exclude points at detected motion. Karimi & Lindenbergh (2014a) rule out direct SIFT with RANSAC against the first image of a helicopter sequence, in part because of the moving vehicles, and chain consecutive homographies instead. Ljubičić et al. (2021a) compare seven stabilization tools on UAV river footage, where the water moves and the banks do not, by residual motion at static features. None of these measures capture or what it costs in position.

Aerial detection benchmarks and trajectory datasets

Aerial object detection has well-established benchmarks (Ding et al., 2022a; Zhu et al., 2022a), DOTA made OBB standard for aerial objects, and UAVid (Lyu et al., 2020a) separates moving from static cars in 4K UAV video for semantic segmentation. They evaluate recognition, not the registration that must precede any use of object positions when the camera moves. Drone-based trajectory datasets show the dependency most clearly: pNEUMA (Barmpounakis & Geroliminis, 2020a), inD (Bock et al., 2020a), CitySim (Zheng et al., 2024a) and Songdo Traffic (Fonod et al., 2025b) all extract positions from hovering footage after a registration step, whose error georeferenced positions (Novikov et al., 2024a) inherit directly, and the intersections they are recorded over are where a moving-object consensus is most likely.

UAV stabilization for traffic monitoring

The work closest to this paper is Fonod et al. (2025b), which extracts georeferenced vehicle trajectories from hovering-drone recordings of urban intersections and stabilizes each frame onto a reference frame with an object-masked homography, releasing that stage as stabilo (Fonod, 2026g) and its parameter study as stabilo-optimize. The vehicles are masked to keep correspondences on moving objects out of the fit, the failure this paper names consensus capture, but the pipeline was selected on static scenes under synthetic warps, so neither that failure nor what masking does about it was measured on the recordings. That is the gap addressed here: the static campaign is extended (Section 6) and paired with a dynamic one on the footage the pipeline is deployed on (Section 7), where the masking axis can be measured rather than assumed.

3 Problem setting

Scene and platform assumptions

Recordings come from hovering drones at approximately constant altitude (140 m to 150 m140\text{\,}\mathrm{m}150\text{\,}\mathrm{m}) in BEV (BEV) at 4K resolution (3840×21603840\times 2160), so inter-frame motion is small and wind-induced. The GSD (GSD) is about 5.5 cm5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} per pixel: the scale of the homographies that register hovers of this experiment onto its georeferenced orthophoto (Fonod et al., 2025b) ranges from 0.05480.0548 to 0.0564 m0.0564\text{\,}\mathrm{m} per pixel over eleven hovers. A pixel of registration error is thus about 5.5 cm5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} on the ground, and the 5 px5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} upper limit of the accuracy interval below is about 28 cm28\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}. Every pixel quantity in this paper converts at that rate. The stabilization model is a reference-frame homography, which holds the static scene in place over a hover exactly only where that scene is planar. Above-ground structures (buildings, poles, vegetation) depart from the plane in proportion to how far the platform translates; a hovering platform translates little but does drift, so the evaluation excludes buildings and large tree canopy, the largest such structures, by polygons drawn on each reference frame (Section 4.3) and scores the rest of the static scene. The deployed regime is a hovering platform, so the geometric perturbation a pipeline has to recover in practice is a few pixels of drift and a fraction of a degree of yaw per frame relative to the reference, growing slowly over a recording. Part I samples a wider regime than that, so that a pipeline’s operating limits are measured, and Section 6 states where the two regimes differ.

3.1 Images, transforms, and the registration model

Let Ω={0,…,W−1}×{0,…,H−1}\Omega=\{0,\dots,W-1\}\times\{0,\dots,H-1\} be the pixel domain of a recording and let Fk:Ω→ℝF^{k}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} denote its kk-th frame, with FrefF^{\mathrm{ref}} a designated reference frame (one fixed frame per case, chosen by the case selection of Section 7.1). Write π⁡(x1,x2,x3)=(x1/x3,x2/x3)\dehom(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=(x_{1}/x_{3},\,x_{2}/x_{3}) for the projection from homogeneous to Euclidean coordinates, and let ℍ\mathbb{H} be the group of planar homographies, that is, the real projective linear group PGL⁡(3,ℝ)\mathrm{PGL}(3,\mathbb{R}) of non-singular 3×33\times 3 matrices identified up to a non-zero scalar (Hartley & Zisserman, 2004a). Table 2 collects the notation. A homography 𝐇∈ℍ\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{H} acts on a point 𝐱∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} by

𝐇⋅𝐱=π⁡(𝐇​[𝐱1]),\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{x}\;=\;\dehom\!\left(\mathbf{H}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right), (1)

which is defined whenever the third homogeneous coordinate is non-zero. A degenerate or non-finite estimate drives that coordinate to zero, and Section 4.6 explains why the resulting non-finite coordinates are propagated rather than suppressed.

Direct-to-reference registration

Each frame FkF^{k} is aligned to FrefF^{\mathrm{ref}} by a homography 𝐇k→ref∈ℍ\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb{H}, estimated directly for every kk; the registered frame samples FkF^{k} through its inverse:

Fref​(𝐱)≈Fk​(𝐇ref→k⋅𝐱),𝐱∈Ω.F^{\mathrm{ref}}(\mathbf{x})\;\approx\;F^{k}\!\left(\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{ref}\rightarrow k}\cdot\mathbf{x}\right),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\Omega. (2)

Sequential accumulation, 𝐇k→ref=∏j=1kHj→j−1\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}=\prod_{j=1}^{k}H^{j\to j-1}, is not used. Its error grows with kk by construction, and it is not the algorithm deployed in reference-frame stabilization (Fonod et al., 2025b). Eq. 2 rests on the ground-plane assumption, which above-ground structure violates.

3.2 Pipelines under study

A pipeline is the complete chain that turns an image pair into a transform. We write it as a tuple

𝒫=(det,desc,match,rob,μ),\mathcal{P}\;=\;(\,\mathrm{det},\ \mathrm{desc},\ \mathrm{match},\ \mathrm{rob},\ \mu\,), (3)

whose components are, in order, the feature detector, the descriptor, the matcher, the robust estimator, and the masking strategy μ∈{none,hbb,obb}\mu\in\{\textsf{none},\textsf{hbb},\textsf{obb}\} of Section 5. Applied to a pair it yields

𝒫⁡(Fref,Fk,ℬref,ℬk)∈ℍ∪{⊥},\mathcal{P}\!\left(F^{\mathrm{ref}},\,F^{k},\,\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{ref}},\,\mathcal{B}^{k}\right)\;\in\;\mathbb{H}\cup\{\bot\}, (4)

where ℬref\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{ref}} and ℬk\mathcal{B}^{k} are the object annotations of the reference frame and of frame kk (Section 5) and ⊥\bot denotes a failure to produce an estimate at all. Admitting ⊥\bot explicitly, rather than substituting the identity, is what makes the failure rate a reported quantity instead of a silent bias (Section 4.6). We write 𝐇^k→ref\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} for a successful estimate.

The five axes of Eq. 3 are evaluated jointly. Component-wise evaluation is the norm in the matching literature, but the quantity a stabilization system delivers is the transform, and the interactions between the axes, particularly between μ\mu and rob\mathrm{rob}, are what this benchmark is designed to expose.

The components come from two libraries: the classical detectors and descriptors and every robust estimator are OpenCV’s, and the learned detectors, descriptors and matchers are kornia’s (Riba et al., 2020a). Both are driven through stabilo (Fonod, 2026g), the stabilization library of Fonod et al. (2025b), which this benchmark evaluates and does not modify. Which implementation supplies a component is part of what is compared, for the reason given below.

Selection of pipelines

The detector axis holds ten pipelines. Five are classical, matched by brute force with a ratio test: ORB (Rublee et al., 2011a), SIFT (Lowe, 2004a), RootSIFT (Arandjelović & Zisserman, 2012a), BRISK (Leutenegger et al., 2011a) and AKAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2013a). Four are learned and sparse: DISK (Tyszkiewicz et al., 2020a), DeDoDe (Edstedt et al., 2024b) and Key.Net (Barroso-Laguna et al., 2019a) (KeyNet in the tables), each matched by LightGlue (Lindenberger et al., 2023a), and XFeat (Potje et al., 2024a), matched by brute force because the library’s LightGlue has no weights for it. One is detector-free, LoFTR (Sun et al., 2021a), which has no keypoint budget to set. The deployed library exposes one more detector, KAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2012a), which is left out: AKAZE is its accelerated variant, and it is the slowest classical detector by a wide margin. Otherwise, the set is everything the library exposes, which is the inclusion criterion: the object of study is the system a trajectory-extraction pipeline actually runs and the alternatives a practitioner can select between by configuration alone, not the state of the art in matching at large. Methods outside that system, such as SuperPoint (DeTone et al., 2018a) and the dense matchers of Section 2, fall outside this scope; nothing in the protocol depends on the method, and it applies to them unchanged.

Robust estimators are identified by implementation, not by name

The rob\mathrm{rob} axis sweeps nine OpenCV method codes spanning seven algorithms: LMEDS (Rousseeuw, 1984a), RANSAC (Fischler & Bolles, 1981a), RHO (Bazargani et al., 2018a), GC-RANSAC (Barath & Matas, 2018a), PROSAC (Chum & Matas, 2005a), MAGSAC++ (Barath et al., 2020a), and LO-RANSAC (Chum et al., 2003a) in three configurations that differ in local-optimization iterations and in whether they run in parallel, the last four within OpenCV’s implementation of the USAC framework (Raguram et al., 2013a). They are reported under OpenCV’s flag names with the algorithm in parentheses, because the three LO-RANSAC configurations are separate entries a practitioner selects from, and because two of the flags are widely described as DEGENSAC, including in the documentation of the library evaluated here, although neither carries the dominant-plane check of Chum et al. (2005a) into a homography estimate (Section 4.1). Following Barath et al. (2023a), a method is fixed by its implementation and version rather than by its published name (Appendix A).

Masking acts on feature detection

The order is: detection or segmentation →\rightarrow mask construction →\rightarrow feature detection →\rightarrow description →\rightarrow matching →\rightarrow robust estimation. No keypoint inside a mask reaches matching, so metrics defined on “removed features” or on a “dynamic inlier ratio” are not applicable here, and are not used. Where the mask enters the detector differs between implementations, and it decides what masking can do under a feature budget; every detector is used with the masking its implementation provides, unmodified. ORB, BRISK and AKAZE detect outside the mask and then keep their strongest responses up to the budget, so the keypoints a mask removes are replaced by others. SIFT, as OpenCV implements it, keeps its strongest responses over the whole frame and then drops those inside the mask; the learned detectors accept no mask, so the library drops their selected keypoints that fall inside it. For both, masking can only remove keypoints.

4 Evaluation methodology

This section shows why the internal statistics of a robust fit cannot rank pipelines on a dynamic scene and defines what replaces them: the metrics, the treatment of failures, comparability, the audit of the reference estimator, and the analysis plan.

4.1 Why internal-consistency metrics are insufficient

Inlier count, inlier ratio, and reprojection error measure the internal consistency of a fit: how well the correspondences the estimator retained agree with the model fitted to them. On static scenes they are already known to be weak proxies for accuracy. Barath et al. (2023a) report that the inlier count depends on image resolution, on the inlier threshold and on the estimator, so that MAGSAC returns far more inliers than its competitors at comparable pose accuracy, and in the tabulation of Jin et al. (2021a, Table 13) the method with the highest inlier ratio, R2D2 at 52.9 %52.9\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, is outperformed downstream by RootSIFT at 39.6 %39.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}.

The claim here is stronger, and it follows from the scene rather than from the estimator. A homography needs four correspondences; a group of objects moving together, such as a stream of vehicles crossing an intersection, supplies hundreds that are mutually consistent under a single transform, the one describing their motion. Their coverage ranges from a small fraction of a high-altitude view to a large share of a low-altitude view over congested lanes, but the estimator weighs their share of the correspondences, not of the area, so even a small coverage can cast many votes. Outliers that form a coherent structure of their own bias a robust estimate toward a compromise between the structures or capture it outright (Stewart, 1997a), and a busy intersection produces that situation persistently. Wherever the moving group wins, every internal-consistency check is satisfied by the wrong answer: these statistics are not merely uninformative but anti-informative. They cannot tell whether it has won; Section 7.3 measures that for the cases studied here.

The estimator cannot detect this failure on its own. Chum et al. (2005a) detect a scene dominated by a single plane with a test inside the estimator, because that case is a degeneracy: the data underconstrain the fundamental matrix, and the deficiency is visible in the sample. A homography fitted to coherently moving objects is fully determined and over-supported; it differs from the intended solution only in which part of the scene it describes, which no individual correspondence encodes. None of the estimators compared here contains a check that could apply: OpenCV runs DEGENSAC only for the fundamental matrix, and the only tests reaching a homography are conditions on the minimal sample (no three collinear points, unchanged orientation), which a stream of vehicles over several lanes satisfies. The information needed, which image content is static, is external to the estimation problem, so the failure has to be handled by the protocol.

These quantities are therefore recorded as diagnostics, to be explained rather than optimized, and never rank a pipeline. What replaces them is the rest of this section: agreement with an external geometry where one exists (Section 4.2), direct measurement of background alignment where one does not (Section 4.3), and two measures that make a moving-object consensus observable, the direction of the error (Section 4.4) and the share of a moving group’s displacement an estimate follows (Section 4.5).

4.2 Geometric metrics

Corner transfer error

Let 𝒞={𝐜1,…,𝐜4}\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{c}_{4}\} be the frame corners, 𝐜1=(0,0)\mathbf{c}_{1}=(0,0), 𝐜2=(W,0)\mathbf{c}_{2}=(W,0), 𝐜3=(W,H)\mathbf{c}_{3}=(W,H), 𝐜4=(0,H)\mathbf{c}_{4}=(0,H). Given a reference transform 𝐇\mathbf{H} and an estimate 𝐇^\widehat{\mathbf{H}} of its inverse direction, a corner sent forward through 𝐇\mathbf{H} and back through 𝐇^\widehat{\mathbf{H}} should return to where it started; the residual is the error. Define the per-corner displacement

𝐝i=𝐇^⋅(𝐇⋅𝐜i)−𝐜i,i=1,…,4,\mathbf{d}_{i}\;=\;\widehat{\mathbf{H}}\cdot\left(\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{c}_{i}\right)\;-\;\mathbf{c}_{i},\qquad i=1,\dots,4, (5)

and summarize it by

CTEmean=14​∑i∥𝐝i∥,CTEmax=maxi⁡∥𝐝i∥,CTErms=(14​∑i∥𝐝i∥2)1/2.\CTEop_{\mathrm{mean}}=\tfrac{1}{4}\textstyle\sum_{i}\lVert\mathbf{d}_{i}\rVert,\qquad\CTEop_{\max}=\max_{i}\lVert\mathbf{d}_{i}\rVert,\qquad\CTEop_{\mathrm{rms}}=\bigl(\tfrac{1}{4}\textstyle\sum_{i}\lVert\mathbf{d}_{i}\rVert^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}. (6)

The CTE (CTE) is measured in pixels, is invariant to the parameterization of the homography, and weights the frame periphery, where a small angular error produces the largest displacement. We keep the displacement vectors of Eq. 5 and not only their norms, because their directions carry the evidence used in Section 4.4.

Two directions must be distinguished. In Part I the perturbation 𝐇\mathbf{H} maps reference →\to warped and the pipeline estimates the inverse, so Eq. 5 applies directly. In Part II the reference estimator 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} and the candidate 𝐇^k→ref\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} both map current →\to reference, so one is inverted first and the disagreement between two same-direction transforms is

𝐝i=𝐇^k→ref⋅(𝐇~ref→k⋅𝐜i)−𝐜i.\mathbf{d}_{i}\;=\;\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}\cdot\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{\mathrm{ref}\rightarrow k}\cdot\mathbf{c}_{i}\right)\;-\;\mathbf{c}_{i}. (7)

Homography estimation accuracy

Following DeTone et al. (2018a) and Efe et al. (2021a), we aggregate over a set of NN trials by the HEA (HEA): the fraction of trials that succeed within a pixel budget ε\varepsilon,

HEAε=1N∑n=1N[𝒫n≠⊥∧CTEmean(n)≤ε].\HEAop_{\varepsilon}\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,\mathcal{P}_{n}\neq\bot\;\wedge\;\CTEop^{(n)}_{\mathrm{mean}}\leq\varepsilon\,\right]. (8)

A failed trial counts in the denominator but never in the numerator, so declining to answer cannot raise accuracy; unlike a mean CTE, the rate is not dominated by one catastrophic trial.

Integrating the accuracy curve

Any single ε\varepsilon is arbitrary: tuning can make a method win at one threshold, yielding several simultaneous states of the art (Efe et al., 2021a). Following Efe et al. (2021a), Jin et al. (2021a) and Barath et al. (2023a), we summarize HEAε\HEAop_{\varepsilon} by the area under its curve, the mAA (mAA) over a threshold interval,

mAA⁡[εlo,εhi]=1εhi−εlo​∫εloεhiHEAε⁡d​ε=1N​∑n=1Nεhi−clip⁡(CTEmean(n),εlo,εhi)εhi−εlo,\mathrm{mAA}\bigl[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}\bigr]\;=\;\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}}\int_{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}}^{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}}\HEAop_{\varepsilon}\;\mathrm{d}\varepsilon\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}-\mathrm{clip}\bigl(\CTEop^{(n)}_{\mathrm{mean}},\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}\bigr)}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}}, (9)

where the right-hand form, which is what we evaluate, is exact because each trial enters HEAε\HEAop_{\varepsilon} as a step in ε\varepsilon; a failed trial’s error is taken as infinite. Each trial contributes linearly in its error inside the interval and nothing beyond it: past a few pixels an estimate is wrong, and how wrong carries little information.

Both parts report mAA⁡[0,5]\mathrm{mAA}[0,5] px as the headline quantity; the cited benchmarks integrate over other ranges and units, so their values are not comparable with these. In Part II the integral is evaluated per case and averaged with equal weight per case, the sampling unit. The reference estimator’s audited residual (Section 4.8) does not raise the lower limit, since integrating from it would still order two candidates a tenth of a pixel apart above it. It is the equivalence margin of the reference-relative pixel metrics (Section 4.9), mAA keeps its margin of 0.010.01, and mAA⁡[εfloor,5]\mathrm{mAA}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}},5] is reported beside the headline as a sensitivity check.

Object-level agreement

Frame corners describe the transform globally; the annotated objects describe where the content of interest actually lands. For each annotated object jj let 𝐪j∈ℝ4×2\mathbf{q}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 2} hold the corners of its box as the reference geometry places them in the reference frame, and 𝐪^j\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{j} the corners of the same box as the candidate places them, each corner transformed on its own. In Part I these are a box of ℬref\mathcal{B}^{\mathrm{ref}} and its round trip through Eq. 5; in Part II they are a box of ℬk\mathcal{B}^{k} carried into the reference frame by 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} and by 𝐇^k→ref\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}. We define two per-object errors,

IoUj=IoU(𝐪j,𝐪^j),OCEj=∥𝐪^¯j−𝐪¯j∥,\IoUop_{j}\;=\;\IoUop\!\left(\mathbf{q}_{j},\,\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{j}\right),\qquad\OCEop_{j}\;=\;\bigl\lVert\bar{\widehat{\mathbf{q}}}_{j}-\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{j}\bigr\rVert, (10)

where IoU⁡(⋅,⋅)\IoUop(\cdot,\cdot) is the ratio of intersection to union area of two convex quadrilaterals and 𝐪¯j=14​∑i𝐪j,i\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{j}=\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{i}\mathbf{q}_{j,i} is the center of box jj. IoUj\IoUop_{j} is threshold-free and bounded in [0,1][0,1]; the OCE (OCE) is measured in pixels and converts to meters through the GSD of Section 3. Over the objects of one frame, each is summarized by its mean (the headline value), standard deviation, quartiles and extremes; the minimum of IoUj\IoUop_{j} and the maximum of OCEj\OCEop_{j} expose a registration that is accurate on average but fails at one edge of the frame, which a mean hides.

The two errors answer different questions. IoUj\IoUop_{j} depends on object size as well as on registration: a displacement that barely changes the overlap of a bus removes much of a motorcycle’s overlap. OCEj\OCEop_{j} does not, and it is the quantity a trajectory-extraction pipeline inherits, since such a pipeline carries each detected box into the reference frame corner by corner and reads the object’s position off the carried quadrilateral. Because 𝐪j\mathbf{q}_{j} and 𝐪^j\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{j} carry the same box, the detector’s localization error cancels, and OCE isolates what registration adds to a trajectory.

Both errors use the OBB for every pipeline, whatever its masking strategy μ\mu, so no candidate is scored on a geometry its own strategy chose; each 𝐪^j\widehat{\mathbf{q}}_{j} is compared as the quadrilateral it becomes, with no rectangle refitted and no axis-aligned hull, which would conflate registration with orientation.

4.3 Reference-free background-alignment metrics

On real footage no true homography exists, so alignment is measured directly: FrefF^{\mathrm{ref}} is compared with the warped current frame Fk∘𝐇^ref→kF^{k}\!\circ\!\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{\mathrm{ref}\rightarrow k} over an evaluation region that excludes the annotated objects and raised structures.

The evaluation region

Write S⊕DrS\oplus D_{r} and S⊖DrS\ominus D_{r} for the morphological dilation and erosion of a pixel set SS by a disc DrD_{r} of radius rr (Soille, 2004a). Let ℳref\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{ref}} be the pixels covered by the reference frame’s annotated objects and ℳk\mathcal{M}^{k} those of the current frame’s, both rasterized in reference coordinates. The region is

ℛ=(𝒱∩ℳref⊕Dτ¯∩ℳk⊕Dτ¯∩𝒢)⊖Dρ,\mathcal{R}\;=\;\Bigl(\mathcal{V}\,\cap\,\overline{\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{ref}}\oplus D_{\tau}}\,\cap\,\overline{\mathcal{M}^{k}\oplus D_{\tau}}\,\cap\,\mathcal{G}\Bigr)\ominus D_{\rho}, (11)

where 𝒱={𝐱∈Ω:𝐇^ref→k⋅𝐱∈Ω}\mathcal{V}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega:\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{\mathrm{ref}\rightarrow k}\cdot\mathbf{x}\in\Omega\} is the set of pixels receiving real data under the warp, less a two-pixel fringe of interpolated values, 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the frame less polygons drawn by hand over the buildings, other raised structures and large contiguous tree canopy of the reference frame, τ\tau is a constant dilation in pixels, and the erosion by DρD_{\rho} keeps the assembled region a margin away from every one of its boundaries: the frame edge, the edge of the warped data, and the dilated objects. Each term is necessary: without 𝒱\mathcal{V} a homography is rewarded for pushing empty area into frame; without the object terms a busier scene scores worse for every pipeline; without 𝒢\mathcal{G} the parallax of roofs and canopy under the platform’s drift is charged to the pipeline; without the erosion, pixels at those boundaries, where the warp interpolates and the masks meet the background, enter the metric. The polygons are drawn once per case, before any of its results are read, and depend on no pipeline.

Two properties keep Eq. 11 from being tunable by the pipeline under test. The region is common to all candidates: ℳk\mathcal{M}^{k} is placed into reference coordinates by the reference estimator’s 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}, never by the candidate’s own 𝐇^k→ref\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}, and only 𝒱\mathcal{V} is candidate-specific, because it must describe the image that candidate produced. And the dilation τ\tau belongs to the protocol: it is a fixed pixel count, independent of the margin by which a pipeline grows its feature-suppression masks (Section 5). |ℛ|/|Ω||\mathcal{R}|/|\Omega| is recorded with every measurement, and a measurement whose region falls below a minimum area fraction is scored as the identity warp (Section 4.6). Part I computes no reference-free measure.

Four complementary measures

Over ℛ\mathcal{R} we compute SSIM (SSIM) (Wang et al., 2004a), ZNCC (ZNCC), MI (MI) (Viola & Wells, 1997a; Maes et al., 1997a), and a magnitude-weighted agreement of gradient orientation (GOS), a normalized form of the gradient terms used in multimodal registration (Pluim et al., 2000a; Haber & Modersitzki, 2006a). Writing A=FrefA=F^{\mathrm{ref}} and B=Fk∘𝐇^ref→kB=F^{k}\!\circ\!\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{\mathrm{ref}\rightarrow k} restricted to ℛ\mathcal{R}, with means A¯,B¯\bar{A},\bar{B} and standard deviations σA,σB\sigma_{A},\sigma_{B},

ZNCC⁡(A,B)=1|ℛ|​σA​σB​∑𝐱∈ℛ(A⁡(𝐱)−A¯)​(B⁡(𝐱)−B¯)∈[−1,1],\ZNCCop(A,B)\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|\,\sigma_{A}\sigma_{B}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{R}}\bigl(A(\mathbf{x})-\bar{A}\bigr)\bigl(B(\mathbf{x})-\bar{B}\bigr)\;\in\;[-1,1], (12)
MI⁡(A,B)=∑a,bpA​B​(a,b)​log2​pA​B​(a,b)pA​(a)​pB​(b),\MIop(A,B)\;=\;\sum_{a,b}p_{AB}(a,b)\,\log_{2}\frac{p_{AB}(a,b)}{p_{A}(a)\,p_{B}(b)}, (13)

in bits, with pA​Bp_{AB} the joint intensity histogram over ℛ\mathcal{R} (64×6464\times 64 bins) and pA,pBp_{A},p_{B} its marginals, and

GOS⁡(A,B)=∑𝐱∈ℛw(𝐱)cos(∠∇A(𝐱)−∠∇B(𝐱))∑𝐱∈ℛw⁡(𝐱)∈[−1,1],w⁡(𝐱)=(∥∇A​(𝐱)∥​∥∇B​(𝐱)∥)1/2,\mathrm{GOS}(A,B)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{R}}w(\mathbf{x})\,\cos\bigl(\angle\nabla A(\mathbf{x})-\angle\nabla B(\mathbf{x})\bigr)}{\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{R}}w(\mathbf{x})}\;\in\;[-1,1],\qquad w(\mathbf{x})=\bigl(\lVert\nabla A(\mathbf{x})\rVert\,\lVert\nabla B(\mathbf{x})\rVert\bigr)^{1/2}, (14)

with Sobel gradients. The weighting makes Eq. 14 usable on aerial asphalt: flat regions, whose gradient direction is arbitrary, contribute nothing, and road markings and curbs dominate; the geometric mean of the two magnitudes keeps a few high-contrast edges from outweighing the rest quadratically.

The four differ in what they tolerate: ZNCC an affine change of intensity, MI any one-to-one remapping, Eq. 14 any monotonically increasing change, and SSIM, which compares local luminance, contrast and structure separately, the least photometric change of the four. Agreement among them is evidence that a measured alignment is not an artifact of one measure’s blind spot.

4.4 Decomposing error along the dominant motion axis

The mechanism studied here leaves a geometric signature: a homography dragged by a moving-object consensus has its error along the direction of motion, whereas ordinary estimation noise has no preferred direction. Measuring that signature makes capture testable.

Recovering the motion axis

Elongated objects such as vehicles travel along their own long axis, so the orientation distribution of the OBB recovers the direction of flow without any correspondence between frames, which matters because the pairs here reach thousands of frames apart and no tracker links their objects. Let θj\theta_{j} be the orientation of the long axis of box jj of the reference frame and aja_{j} its area. Orientations are axial data: a box rotated by π\pi is the same box, so the mean is taken over doubled angles and halved back (Mardia & Jupp, 1999a). With the weighted resultant

R=∑jaj​e 2​i​θj∑jaj,θ¯=12​arg⁡R,κ=|R|∈[0,1],R\;=\;\frac{\sum_{j}a_{j}\,e^{\,2i\theta_{j}}}{\sum_{j}a_{j}},\qquad\bar{\theta}=\tfrac{1}{2}\arg R,\qquad\kappa=\lvert R\rvert\in[0,1], (15)

the dominant axis is the unit vector 𝐮=(cos⁡θ¯,sin⁡θ¯)\mathbf{u}=(\cos\bar{\theta},\sin\bar{\theta}) and κ\kappa is its concentration.

Decomposing the error

With 𝐮⟂=(−sin⁡θ¯,cos⁡θ¯)\mathbf{u}^{\perp}=(-\sin\bar{\theta},\cos\bar{\theta}) and the corner displacements 𝐝i\mathbf{d}_{i} of Eq. 7, define

e∥=14​∑i|𝐝i⋅𝐮|,e⟂=14​∑i|𝐝i⋅𝐮⟂|,A=e∥e∥+e⟂∈[0,1].e_{\parallel}=\tfrac{1}{4}\textstyle\sum_{i}\lvert\mathbf{d}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{u}\rvert,\qquad e_{\perp}=\tfrac{1}{4}\textstyle\sum_{i}\lvert\mathbf{d}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{u}^{\perp}\rvert,\qquad A\;=\;\frac{e_{\parallel}}{e_{\parallel}+e_{\perp}}\;\in\;[0,1]. (16)

A≈0.5A\approx 0.5 is isotropic error; A→1A\to 1 is error almost entirely along the motion axis, the signature of a moving-object consensus; and A→0A\to 0 is error across it, which that mechanism cannot produce. Error without a preferred direction need not give A=0.5A=0.5 at four corners, however: a small rotation about the frame center displaces each corner perpendicular to its diagonal and a small scale change along it, so on a 16:916{:}9 frame with 𝐮\mathbf{u} along an image axis they give AA of about 0.360.36 and 0.640.64. The level of AA is therefore read against the identity transform, whose error is the platform’s own motion, and the evidence for capture is an increase of AA without masking over AA with masking on the same pairs, not its level.

The bounded form is used instead of the bare ratio e∥/e⟂e_{\parallel}/e_{\perp}, which diverges exactly in the case of interest (e⟂=0e_{\perp}=0) and would drop the strongest evidence from every aggregate. At a crossroads with two busy perpendicular approaches the doubled angles cancel and κ\kappa falls toward zero, so the decomposition is suppressed when κ<κmin=0.3\kappa<\kappa_{\min}=0.3 rather than reporting an artifact. Eq. 15 also needs oriented annotations, since an HBB carries no orientation.

4.5 Measuring capture directly

The direction of the error is a signature of capture read at the four frame corners, far from the objects that cause it. Capture can also be measured where it happens. The reference frame’s objects are found again in frame kk by the procedure the case selection uses (Section 7.1): each box is compared by appearance with the boxes of similar size in frame kk and accepted only as a mutual best match. With 𝐲j\mathbf{y}_{j} the center of the match of reference box jj, its displacement with the platform’s motion removed by the reference estimator is

𝐦j=𝐇~k→ref⋅𝐲j−𝐪¯j.\mathbf{m}_{j}\;=\;\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}\cdot\mathbf{y}_{j}\;-\;\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{j}. (17)

A box has moved when ∥𝐦j∥\lVert\mathbf{m}_{j}\rVert exceeds a tenth of the median object width: clear of the apparent motion of a stationary object, which comes from box placement and the reference estimator’s error, and less than a car covers between consecutive frames at urban speeds. Moved objects move together with moved object ii when their displacements differ from 𝐦i\mathbf{m}_{i} by at most a tenth of the median object width or a quarter of ∥𝐦i∥\lVert\mathbf{m}_{i}\rVert, whichever is larger: the members of one stream drift apart in proportion to how far it moved, while opposing or crossing streams never agree. The largest set by area that moves together with one of its members is the group, GG, the structure a single wrong homography could fit. The capture fraction of a candidate is the share of the group’s displacement it follows,

λ=medianj∈G−(𝐇^k→ref⋅𝐲j−𝐇~k→ref⋅𝐲j)⋅𝐦j∥𝐦j∥2.\lambda\;=\;\operatorname*{median}_{j\in G}\;\frac{-\bigl(\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}\cdot\mathbf{y}_{j}-\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}\cdot\mathbf{y}_{j}\bigr)\cdot\mathbf{m}_{j}}{\lVert\mathbf{m}_{j}\rVert^{2}}. (18)

An estimate that agrees with the reference estimator where the group lies has λ=0\lambda=0; one that registers the group back onto where it stood in the reference frame, which is what a homography fitted to the group does, has λ=1\lambda=1; values between are a compromise fit, pulled toward the group without registering it. A measurement is captured when λ≥0.1\lambda\geq 0.1: the estimate has moved, where the group lies, by at least a tenth of the group’s displacement. That lies above what a transform reaches without following the group: the identity, which uses no features, reaches 0.070.07 from the platform’s motion alone, and the reference estimator’s audited error (Section 7.2) amounts to 0.080.08 on the smallest displacement of any group, 5 px5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (Table 7). Capture is reported descriptively, with the counts at λ≥0.25\lambda\geq 0.25, 0.50.5 and 11 beside it (files offline_masking_capture.csv and realtime_masking_capture.csv; the CSV files named in this paper are released with its data (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026b)). λ\lambda is defined on pairs whose group holds at least four objects, and only where the pipeline returned an estimate. Beside it, every measurement records where the estimate’s inliers lie: the share on annotated objects and the share on objects that moved. The second undercounts what moves with the objects, since a vehicle’s cast shadow lies outside its box; λ\lambda does not depend on it. These quantities are diagnostics, like the inlier statistics they are read against, and never rank a pipeline.

4.6 Treatment of failures

A registration pipeline can fail outright: too few matches survive filtering, or the robust estimator returns a degenerate transform. Implementations commonly substitute the identity, the stabilization library evaluated here among them (Fonod, 2026g), which keeps a campaign running but hides the failure and biases every metric, because the identity is a plausible answer for a nearly stationary drone. We therefore admit ⊥\bot explicitly in Eq. 4 and detect it from what the estimator returns: an absent inlier count, which every fallback leaves, or a missing or non-finite matrix. An estimate exactly equal to the identity is not a failure, since between near-identical frames the estimator returns exactly the identity with thousands of inliers, and that answer is correct. A finite estimate that drives the third homogeneous coordinate of Eq. 1 to zero at a corner yields non-finite coordinates, which Eqs. 8 and 9 score as a miss; clamping that division, as some implementations do, would score a collapsing estimate as merely inaccurate.

The reference-free measures need a different treatment, because an undefined value drops out of a mean: a pipeline that failed on a third of its pairs would otherwise report its background alignment over the two thirds it solved. A failed pair is therefore scored with the identity warp, the transform the pipeline actually delivered, and so is a pair whose evaluation region is too small to be read; declining to answer costs exactly what delivering the identity costs.

A configuration that exhausts the benchmark machine’s memory is not a failure. It is reported as not available and its partial measurements are discarded, because a sparser scene needs less memory and is also easier to register, so the subset that fit would flatter it. Counting it as a failure would make a score depend on the machine’s memory.

4.7 Placing pipelines on equal footing

A benchmark that compares ten pipelines at one shared set of matcher settings measures the settings as much as the pipelines. This is the central methodological finding of the benchmarks reviewed in Section 2, and we adopt their remedies.

Two hyperparameters are tuned per pipeline

The ratio-test threshold and the inlier threshold of the robust estimator are both known to be decisive and to have method-specific optima: the first thresholds a descriptor distance distribution, a property of the descriptor, and the second a reprojection residual, a property of keypoint localization accuracy. Efe et al. (2021a) obtain their entire result by varying the first; Jin et al. (2021a, Sec. 5.3) find its optimum differs per feature. They are swept jointly rather than sequentially (the inlier threshold alone where the matcher applies no ratio test: LightGlue and LoFTR), following Barath et al. (2023a): a looser ratio test admits more outliers, which moves the inlier threshold that best separates them, so the sequential optimum need not be the joint one. Selection uses Eq. 9, the quantity the benchmark ranks on, because the threshold maximizing correspondence-level accuracy is not the one maximizing homography accuracy: a robust estimator turns a surplus of looser matches into a better fit (Efe et al., 2021a). It is also conservative: a pipeline keeps the values its preset carries unless the best grid point beats them on mAA by more than the equivalence margin of 0.010.01 (Section 4.9), because where the optimum is flat the best grid point only moves the values within a set the data cannot tell apart; Part II starts from Part I’s values in the same way.

The remaining estimator parameters are fixed, on published grounds

Of the three parameters every robust estimator here exposes, the confidence level, the inlier threshold and an iteration cap, only the threshold is tuned. Jin et al. (2021a, Sec. 5.1) “find the confidence value to be the least sensitive” of the three and fix it at 1−10−61-10^{-6}, the value used here. The iteration cap is a time budget rather than an accuracy parameter, and the benchmarks we follow treat it as one: Barath et al. (2023a) fix it at 10001000 while grid-searching the thresholds and sweep it only to draw a time–accuracy curve, and Jin et al. (2021a) set it from a per-pair time budget. We fix it at 50005000, where it is not the binding constraint, and report wall-clock time so that no pipeline gains accuracy through unreported computation. All remaining parameters are held at documented values across pipelines (Appendix A).

Tuning and evaluation scenes are disjoint

The sweep runs on scenes held out from every reported result, a split the benchmark’s tooling enforces: a threshold chosen on the data a number is reported on measures how much tuning freedom each pipeline was granted, and Barath et al. (2023a) name the lack of such a split as a drawback of earlier homography datasets. The split is by site, not by frame: the Part I set holds eight intersections recorded by more than one drone, near-duplicate views of the same road layout, markings and parked vehicles, so a frame-wise split would leak the evaluation scenes into the tuning half. Every third site in alphabetical order goes to tuning, which reproduces the split from the file names alone. Of the 2929 scenes, 99 from 77 sites tune and 2020 from 1313 sites evaluate. Part II keeps the split: its evaluation cases are drawn from evaluation sites and its own tuning cases from tuning sites. Tuning is run with masking disabled and the same parameters are used under every masking mode, so no mode is tuned into its own best configuration; because the deployed configuration is masked, this is the conservative choice for the masking comparison, and any advantage measured for masking is measured with parameters tuned against it.

The compute budget is fixed before anything is tuned

Two further parameters, the downsampling ratio and the feature budget, decide how much work a pipeline does rather than how it uses it, and the shipped presets do not hand every pipeline the same amount: the learned models’ ratios are memory bounds. Jin et al. (2021a) report every method at matched keypoint budgets for this reason, and Barath et al. (2023a) report accuracy against runtime. We therefore sweep both parameters over every pipeline on the tuning scenes first, under masking disabled and under OBB masking, and read off a single matched operating point: the lowest budget at which every pipeline that can reach it is within the equivalence margin of its own saturation under both masking conditions. Masking removes the highest-contrast content in the frame, so the saturating budget need not be the same with and without it. If no budget on the grid meets the criterion, every pipeline runs at the largest one and its shortfall from saturation is reported. The thresholds are then selected at that operating point, so that what is tuned is what is run; a pipeline that cannot reach it on the benchmark machine is reported as such rather than scored at a lower budget. Part II runs at two other points of the same grid, one for offline and one for real-time registration (Section 7.1); its thresholds are tuned again at each and stated in pixels of the downsampled frame, so that they keep their size relative to keypoint localization as the frame shrinks.

4.8 Auditing the reference estimator

Part II has no true homography, so a strong pipeline is used as a reference estimator 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} (Section 7.2). This is pseudo-ground truth: every Part II number is a comparison against an estimate that has its own error, and one drawn from the same family as the candidates cannot be assumed neutral between them (Brachmann et al., 2021a). We measure that error against independent control points rather than assuming it negligible.

A set of unambiguous ground-plane GCP is chosen by hand in FrefF^{\mathrm{ref}} and located in a subset of sampled frames, as described below. For a label ℓ\ell present in both, with 𝐩ℓref\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\ell} and 𝐩ℓk\mathbf{p}^{k}_{\ell} its annotated positions, the residual is

rℓ=∥𝐇~k→ref⋅𝐩kℓ−𝐩refℓ∥,r_{\ell}\;=\;\bigl\lVert\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}\cdot\mathbf{p}^{k}_{\ell}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\ell}\bigr\rVert, (19)

and the upper percentile of its distribution pooled over frames is a resolution floor

εfloor=Q0.95​({rℓ}).\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}}\;=\;Q_{0.95}\bigl(\{r_{\ell}\}\bigr). (20)

Differences between candidates smaller than εfloor\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}} lie within the reference estimator’s own uncertainty and are not interpreted as evidence.

Because the GCP depend on no pipeline, Eq. 19 applies equally to a candidate 𝐇^k→ref\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}, and this is the comparison the masking result rests on. The reference runs with OBB masking, the configuration expected to be most accurate, so a candidate run under the same masking shares its feature population (the same background pixels, the same exclusions, the same movers the detector missed), and its error is positively correlated with the reference’s: its disagreement with the reference understates its true error, while an unmasked candidate shares less and carries more of the reference’s error on top of its own. A masking comparison read off reference-relative numbers is therefore biased toward the reference’s own masking mode, and for the reference’s own detector under OBB masking it is circular by construction; Eq. 20 measures the reference’s absolute error on the audited points but says nothing about that covariance. The GCP break the dependence. On every audited frame we fit a homography to the points themselves,

𝐇k→refGCP=arg​min𝐇∈ℍ∑ℓ∥𝐇⋅𝐩kℓ−𝐩refℓ∥2,\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{GCP}}\;=\;\argmin_{\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{H}}\sum_{\ell}\bigl\lVert\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathbf{p}^{k}_{\ell}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\ell}\bigr\rVert^{2}, (21)

by the normalized direct linear transform with a nonlinear refinement of the reprojection error (Hartley & Zisserman, 2004a), from at least 1212 points spread to the frame periphery: the number and placement of control points govern accuracy in UAV photogrammetry (Sanz-Ablanedo et al., 2018a), and a homography fitted to central points is poorly determined exactly where the CTE is read. Its error depends on no pipeline. Every candidate is scored against 𝐇GCPk→ref\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{GCP}} on the audited frames with the metrics of Section 4.2, and those scores, with the reference-free measures, are the primary evidence for the masking comparison; the reference-relative scores over all pairs remain the evidence for behavior with temporal distance and for ranking detectors within one masking mode, where whatever the reference’s OBB masking favors is common to every candidate compared. The tables of these scores flag SIFT and RootSIFT, which share the reference’s keypoint detector and whose reference-relative scores are therefore the least independent of it.

Placement of the points

Points are placed in a magnified panel with an exact pixel mapping. In FrefF^{\mathrm{ref}} they are chosen and annotated manually, on the road surface, clear of every object and of the excluded structure. In each audited frame every point is first proposed by an image fit that shares nothing with the candidates or the reference estimator: the point’s 81×81$81$\times$81$-pixel neighborhood in FrefF^{\mathrm{ref}}, with the objects of both frames filled with the background mean, is aligned to the frame by an affine enhanced correlation coefficient fit (Evangelidis & Psarakis, 2008a) started from the platform motion of the case selection (Section 7.1), and the proposal stands only if the fit correlates at 0.80.8 or better and the fit back from it returns within half a pixel of the reference point. The annotator sees each proposal beside the point’s reference neighborhood and accepts it or places the point manually instead; a dense local fit and a sparse whole-frame homography fail in different ways, so their agreement is evidence about the estimator, and the review guards against the failures of the fit itself (a neighboring feature, an occlusion, a point that left the frame). A point without a standing proposal is placed by hand in a panel that opens near where 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} predicts it, displaced by a hidden offset of a few pixels, so that a click following the panel rather than the feature can only inflate the residual. On two cases the audited frames were also placed entirely by hand (Table 6): pooled over both, the unaided clicks lie a median of 0.44 px0.44\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (0.82 px0.82\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at the 9595th percentile) from the proposals and 0.46 px0.46\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (0.91 px0.91\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}) from 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}’s predictions, while the proposals lie 0.06 px0.06\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (0.32 px0.32\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}) from the predictions; on each case the proposals lie closer to the predictions than either lies to the clicks, which separates the click noise from the estimator’s error. The GCP repeatability is measured by annotating the audited frames of two cases a second time in a separate session without proposals, the reference frame included; it is the annotation floor, reported beside Eq. 20 so the two are not conflated. The residual is reported per temporal-offset bin as well as pooled, because the reference’s error plausibly grows with offset as shadows move and content turns over; the first of the four audit bins holds offsets of one to three frames, at which a moving group is still shared with the reference, so that a captured estimate can be scored against the GCP as well.

Finally, the evaluation region of Eq. 11 places the current frame’s objects with 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}, so a reference error of ε\varepsilon misplaces the object exclusion by ε\varepsilon. The dilation τ\tau absorbs that only while τ>εfloor\tau>\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}}, so the reference-free family uses the reference only to place the exclusion, which still covers the objects while that holds; the implementation checks the audited residual against τ\tau and warns when the condition fails. A candidate’s own error is not absorbed: a misregistered frame carries its objects off their exclusion, and their pixels enter its own score.

4.9 Analysis plan

The plan below was fixed before the campaigns it governs ran, and the implementation applies it when it renders a table, so that no number is bolded, ranked, or called a difference by a rule chosen after the outcome was seen. Like the comparisons of learning methods over several data sets (Demšar, 2006a), it treats the independent unit, not the measurement, as the sample, and uses paired nonparametric tests over it.

Units and clusters

In Part I one measurement is a (scene, trial) pair. The perturbation depends on the scene and the trial only, never on the pipeline, so pipelines are compared on paired per-trial differences. The independent unit is the site, of which the evaluation set has 1313: two frames of one intersection from two drones show the same static scene and are not independent evidence. In Part II one measurement is a frame pair under one pipeline and one masking mode. Masking is a within-pair factor, since all three modes see the same pair, so the masking effect is a paired difference per pair. The independent unit is the case, of which there are nine, and frame pairs within a case are never treated as independent. The nine lie at seven intersections, two of them hovered over in two sessions; a case is defined by the traffic at its reference frame, which two sessions do not share, so the case rather than the intersection is the unit.

Outcomes

Part I ranks on mAA⁡[0,5]\mathrm{mAA}[0,5] of Eq. 9. The Part II masking claim has one primary contrast, OBB masking against none for the average pipeline (per case, the mean paired benefit over the pipelines measured on every outcome in every case), on five outcomes: the CTE against 𝐇GCPk→ref\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{GCP}} on the audited frames, the reference-free ZNCC and gradient-orientation agreement over the evaluation region on all pairs, and IoU (IoU) and OCE against 𝐇GCPk→ref\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{GCP}} on the audited frames. The contrast is claimed when at least one outcome favors OBB masking after a Holm adjustment (Holm, 1979a) across the five and none favors no masking at the unadjusted level; the second condition can only withhold a claim. The outcomes differ in sensitivity: those against 𝐇GCPk→ref\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{GCP}} see eight audited frames per case, the reference-free ones every pair, so requiring all five to agree would tie the claim to the least sensitive. Secondary are the same contrast per pipeline, and horizontal against none and oriented against horizontal, both for the average pipeline and per pipeline. The mechanism claim has three pre-specified contrasts, each formed within a case and then read across cases: the oriented-against-none benefit increases with the coverage of the current frame; it is smaller in pairs whose foreground did not move than in pairs whose foreground did, at matched coverage (Section 7.1); and the motion alignment AA of Eq. 16 is larger without masking than with OBB masking. Each is read for the average pipeline, as the primary contrast is, with a Holm adjustment across its outcomes (ZNCC and gradient-orientation agreement for the first two, AA for the third), and is supported when an outcome’s interval lies above zero at an adjusted pp of at most 0.050.05; the per-pipeline readings are secondary. Capture itself is reported descriptively, per pipeline, masking mode and offset bin: the share of pairs with a moving group on which the estimate is captured (Eq. 18), the cases in which that happens, and the inlier count and ratio of captured estimates beside those of the others. It depends on the traffic each case happens to carry at its reference frame, so it describes these cases and is not tested as a population rate.

Estimates and intervals

Every comparison reports the paired difference as an effect size: the Hodges–Lehmann estimate (Hodges & Lehmann, 1963a) of the per-cluster paired differences, with a 95 %95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} percentile bootstrap interval (Davison & Hinkley, 1997a) obtained by resampling sites in Part I and cases in Part II, with 10 00010\,000 draws. Every outcome, mAA included, is computed per cluster and differenced there, so an interval on mAA is an interval on the cluster-level paired difference. The test is an exact sign-flip permutation (Good, 2005a) of the per-cluster paired differences: 2132^{13} flips in Part I and 29=5122^{9}=512 in Part II, so the smallest two-sided pp attainable in Part II is 2/512=0.00392/512=0.0039. After the Holm adjustment across five outcomes, a masking effect is detectable at the 0.050.05 level only if it has the same sign in all nine cases, or in eight with the dissenting case the smallest in magnitude (4/512×5=0.0394/512\times 5=0.039). The design detects a consistent effect and nothing weaker. The 2×22\times 2 over moving foreground and coherence, with two cases per cell, is reported descriptively, without intervals or an interaction test; the within-case mechanism contrasts test its prediction.

Criterion for a difference

A difference is claimed only when the bootstrap interval excludes zero and the point estimate exceeds an equivalence margin δ\delta, the smallest difference worth acting on (Lakens, 2017a). In Part I the ground truth is exact and δ=0.01\delta=0.01 in mAA, one percent of its [0,1][0,1] range, so that two thousand paired trials cannot declare a difference no reader would act on. In Part II, reference-relative pixel metrics use the audited residual, δ=εfloor\delta=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}}, which for a comparison pooled over the cases is the largest of the per-case residuals; pixel metrics against 𝐇GCPk→ref\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{GCP}} use the 9595th percentile of the GCP repeatability, the larger of the two repeat sessions’; and IoU and the reference-free measures use no margin, since their units carry no floor, and are reported with intervals alone.

Multiplicity and presentation

Part I has one primary outcome, mAA, and Part II one primary contrast. Secondary contrasts are reported with intervals and Holm-adjusted pp-values (per pipeline, across the pipelines) and mark the differences that pass the rule above, but carry no claim. Every table bolds the best value in a column and every value not distinguishable from it under the rule above, and says so in its caption; columns that are diagnostics are never bolded. Bolding applies the rule without a multiplicity adjustment and is descriptive: it establishes neither equivalence within the bold set nor an adjusted difference outside it. The estimate, interval and adjusted pp behind each of those decisions are reported in Appendix D. The correlation between inlier ratio and alignment quality (Fig. 10) is computed within each pipeline and case and its distribution is shown, never a single pooled coefficient, because estimators differ systematically in how many inliers they report at equal accuracy (Barath et al., 2023a) and a pooled correlation would measure that mix.

5 Masking configurations and their annotations

Three configurations are evaluated, and the complete benchmark is repeated for each: no masking, HBB masks, and OBB masks. Under the latter two, the annotated boxes of both frames are rasterized into a binary mask that the feature detector receives, so that no keypoint is detected on an annotated object; an HBB is rasterized as an axis-aligned rectangle and an OBB as a quadrilateral. Each box is first scaled about its center by 1+m1+m with the mask margin m=0.15m=$0.15$, to absorb annotation slack, shadow and motion blur at the object boundary. That margin belongs to the pipeline and is a hyperparameter of it, distinct from the constant dilation τ\tau of the evaluation region in Eq. 11, which belongs to the protocol. The HBB is the detector’s and the OBB is fitted to the segmented vehicle, so the two differ in extent as well as in shape and neither need contain the other; the suppressed-area gap between the two geometries is reported for every scene set.

Rationale for two box geometries

Whether the shape of a mask matters for registration is not obvious in advance, and plausible mechanisms point both ways. An HBB around a vehicle turned off the image axes also covers the road beside it, two wedges of asphalt that at an intersection often hold lane markings, stop lines and curb edges, the static texture the estimator most needs; the wedges grow with the angle, to about twice the vehicle’s own area for a 4040×\times1010 box at 45 °45\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}, and in a queue of turning vehicles adjacent HBB merge over the markings between them. OBB keep that texture. Conversely, what moves with a vehicle is not confined to its body: its cast shadow, its motion blur and the reflections off its windows travel with it, lie partly outside a tight OBB, and supply correspondences that agree with its motion, and the extra area of an HBB covers part of them. Which effect dominates, if either, is an empirical question, so the box geometry is a controlled axis of both parts, and the margin sweep of Section 7.5 compares the two geometries at equal suppressed area, so that a difference can be told apart from the area each removes. OBB are also what the motion axis of Section 4.4 and the object-level errors of Section 4.2 are read from, whatever the masking.

The annotations are the same for both parts and are produced outside the benchmark, once per image set, by the detector released with geo-trax (Fonod, 2026d) for the HBB and by the conversion of Appendix E for the oriented ones. Neither model runs inside the benchmark loop: a campaign re-reads the same frames tens of thousands of times, and two pipelines are only comparable if they were handed identical masks, which a per-run detector call cannot promise.
