Each label set carries a provenance record naming the command, the settings, the package versions and the checkpoint checksums that produced it, because annotations are not bit-reproducible across accelerators and the published annotations, not the command, are the reproducible artifact.

5.1 Oriented annotations and the Songdo Vision OBB release

OBB masks require an oriented annotation for every object in every frame the benchmark touches, orders of magnitude beyond what can be drawn by hand. They are obtained from the horizontal annotations by prompting SAM-family segmentation models (Kirillov et al., 2023a; Ravi et al., 2025a) with each box and fitting a minimum-area rotated rectangle (Freeman & Shapira, 1975a) to the resulting mask (Fonod, 2026e); the procedure and its validation against a human-verified oriented reference are given in Appendix E. Inside the benchmark the conversion runs over the vehicle annotations of the scenes and cases under test, the only use on which any number in this paper depends. Applied to the whole of Songdo Vision (Fonod et al., 2026a) at the selected configuration it yields 274 190274\,190 OBB over 54195419 frames, one per HBB and carrying its class and identifier, released as Songdo Vision OBB (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026c) with the human-verified reference used to select and validate the conversion: 42454245 OBB over 5050 frames from six recordings (Section E.1). None of those 5050 frames appears in Songdo Vision, as checked against all 54195419 by checksum and by decoded pixels, but they come from the same six flights. That is a weaker guarantee than the site-level split of Section 4.7, and the appropriate one here: the conversion is selected by IoU against a human-verified reference, a quantity that involves neither the pipelines nor their metrics, so scene overlap cannot tune it toward a favorable stabilization result; it can only flatter the reported conversion fidelity, which Appendix E therefore states as a tuned-set estimate.

Fallback boxes

Where the segmentation finds no usable mask inside a box, the source HBB is emitted unchanged, which would dilute any difference between the two mask geometries. At the selected configuration that share is 00 wherever it has been measured: among the 42454245 boxes of the reference set, the 274 190274\,190 of the released conversion, and, read from the per-object confidence written beside each label file (exactly 00 marks a fallback), the 23112311 boxes of Part I’s 2929 scenes, the 60 21360\,213 of Part II’s nine cases and the 44 39744\,397 of its five tuning cases (136136 frames each).

6 Part I: static benchmark

6.1 Protocol

Fig. 2 shows the protocol. Known homographies (translation, rotation about the frame center, uniform scale, and a small projective term) and a chain of photometric degradations (brightness, saturation, blur, haze, sensor noise, and JPEG compression) are applied to static aerial frames, and the pipeline registers the degraded, warped frame back onto the original, so the ground truth is exact. Trials are paired: the perturbation of a (scene, trial) does not depend on the pipeline, so every pipeline faces the identical sequence of perturbations, and every sampled parameter is recorded with its trial. The ranges (Table 1) are those of the published campaign (Fonod et al., 2025b): translation up to 10 %10\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of each frame dimension, rotation up to 15 °15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}, scale within 5 %5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, and a small projective term. This is wider than the deployed hover regime of Section 3, so that operating limits are measured; a second configuration at deployment scale (rotation within 2 °2\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}, translation within 2 %2\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, scale within 1 %1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, no projective term, the same photometric chain) is run for the detector axis, and rotation is swept separately beyond the main range.

The masks for the warped copy are the scene’s boxes carried through the known homography, since the warped frame has no annotation of its own. An OBB stays a quadrilateral; an HBB for the warped frame is the axis-aligned envelope of the carried OBB, which is what a detector would draw around the rotated object, rather than of the carried HBB, which would inflate an envelope a second time by an amount growing with the rotation.

Fig. 3 shows one trial. Vehicles are among the most textured content of a road scene, and without masking a large share of a pipeline’s inliers lies on them. In Part I that is harmless, because the vehicles move with the ground; under masking, a detector that applies the mask before its keypoint cap (Section 3.2) spends that share of its budget on the ground instead. In Part II these are the correspondences a moving group can contribute.

The campaigns run in a fixed order on the two splits of Section 4.7. On the tuning scenes: the compute-budget sweep, under masking disabled and OBB masking, which fixes the matched operating point; then the joint sweep of the ratio-test and inlier thresholds at that point. On the evaluation scenes, at the selected values: the detector axis under the three masking modes, the same axis at the untuned starting thresholds without masking, which measures the effect of tuning on data it was not selected on, the detector axis again at deployment-scale perturbation, the estimator axis at two fixed detectors, and the rotation sweep. Trial counts are 3030 per scene for the tuning-side sweeps, 100100 for the evaluation campaigns and 5050 for the rotation sweep.

Scene set and selection rule

Part I runs on 2929 4K frames from the hovering sessions of a multi-drone experiment over the Songdo International Business District, South Korea: the static scene set of Section 3.5.2 of Fonod et al. (2025b), byte-identical to the frames that campaign ran on, whose intersections are shown in its Fig. 1. The annotation is regenerated rather than inherited, and the frames are published for the first time with the accompanying data record (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026b). All 2929 come from one session and are selected by a positional rule: the first frame of the first hover of every drone-intersection pair flown in it. Each drone alternates between two or three intersections during a session, and eight of the 2020 intersections are covered in turn by more than one drone, so the 1010 drones record them from 2929 viewpoints. The set is a census of the session’s viewpoints rather than a sample chosen for content: no frame was kept for being busy, quiet, hard or easy, none was removed after the fact, and the rule reproduces the set from the file names alone. Table 3 describes the evaluation frames: object count and covered area each vary by a factor of about four, so the masking cost is measured over a range of densities, and the gap between the two area columns is how much more of the frame an HBB mask suppresses than an oriented one.

6.2 Results

Part I asks which settings of a registration pipeline matter when nothing in the scene moves. The results follow the settings in the order of their effect: the compute budget, the ratio-test and inlier thresholds, and the robust estimator; then the ranking they produce at the operating point and what masking costs. The estimator, deployment and rotation sweeps are given in full in Appendix B.

The compute budget sets the accuracy

The budget sweep crossed four downsampling ratios (0.180.18, 0.300.30, 0.500.50, 1.01.0) with three feature budgets (10001000, 20002000, 80008000) on the tuning scenes, at the untuned starting thresholds, since it precedes the tuning (Fig. 4), and it has the largest effect of the settings in this part. No budget met the criterion of Section 4.7, so every pipeline runs at the grid’s ceiling, full resolution with 80008000 features, and the pipelines fall into two groups below it. ORB, XFeat, KeyNet with LightGlue, BRISK and AKAZE are still gaining at the ceiling: from half to full resolution at 80008000 features their unmasked mAA rises by 0.0350.035, 0.0480.048, 0.0230.023, 0.0180.018 and 0.0170.017, so a lower operating point would rank them below their capacity. SIFT, RootSIFT, DISK and DeDoDe with LightGlue have saturated by half resolution and move by less than the equivalence margin beyond it. LoFTR, which has no feature budget, cannot reach the operating point: at full resolution it exhausts the 24 GB24\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{B} of the benchmark GPU (an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090) and is reported as N/A throughout Part I; below that it scores an mAA of 0.9260.926 at ratios of 0.500.50 and 0.300.30 and 0.8790.879 at its shipped ratio of 0.180.18. OBB masking changes mAA by at most 0.0650.065 at any grid point. The largest change is ORB’s gain at a ratio of 0.180.18 with 10001000 features, which shrinks to 0.0170.017 at 20002000 features and 0.0040.004 at 80008000; the largest loss is XFeat’s, 0.0340.034 at full resolution with 10001000 features. Since nothing in these scenes moves, any such gain is a matter of which features the budget keeps, a point Section 7.5 returns to. At Part II’s real-time point, six of the ten pipelines (ORB, AKAZE, XFeat, SIFT, RootSIFT and DISK with LightGlue) estimate a 4K frame’s transform within one frame interval (33.4 ms33.4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}, median over the tuning scenes) on the benchmark machine, with or without masking. The time covers downsampling, feature extraction under the mask, matching and the robust fit, not decoding, detection, box conversion or warping.

The matcher thresholds have little effect at the operating point

The ratio test and the inlier threshold are the two parameters that earlier benchmarks found decisive (Efe et al., 2021a; Jin et al., 2021a), and they are swept jointly for every pipeline (Section 4.7), from untuned starting values: the ratio of 0.90.9 that the stabilization library ships and an inlier threshold of 22 to 3 px3\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} per detector, listed with the selected values in Table 1. At the operating point the surfaces are flat. All 8080 grid points of SIFT, RootSIFT, ORB, BRISK and AKAZE lie within the equivalence margin of the best, against 5757 of XFeat’s; LightGlue applies no ratio test, so its three pipelines are swept over the threshold alone, and all 88 of their points are tied. Tuning raises mAA over the starting values by 0.00620.0062 for XFeat and by at most 0.00110.0011 for every other pipeline. The incumbents are the values each preset carries, and every pipeline keeps them, since no grid point beats them by more than the margin; the largest gain on offer is 0.00020.0002, for AKAZE at a ratio of 0.80.8. At the kept ratio the inlier threshold moves mAA by at most 0.00020.0002 for every pipeline, so the data do not identify it. The estimator is the reason (Fig. 1): MAGSAC++, the operating estimator, marginalizes over the noise scale instead of committing to one threshold. Below a ratio of 0.700.70 mAA stays flat for SIFT, RootSIFT, AKAZE and BRISK and falls for ORB and XFeat, so the kept ratios lie on the plateau rather than at an edge of it.

The selection carries over to the evaluation scenes. Unmasked, every pipeline’s evaluation-set mAA (Table 4) differs from its tuning-set mAA by at most 0.00250.0025, the largest drop being KeyNet with LightGlue’s, about a quarter of the equivalence margin, and the order of the pipelines is unchanged except that SIFT and RootSIFT, 0.00010.0001 apart on the tuning scenes, swap places. Run at the starting values on the evaluation scenes (file detectors_default_static.csv), the pipelines score lower by 0.00340.0034 for XFeat and differ by at most 0.00110.0011 for the other eight, and the only change of rank is that SIFT and RootSIFT, 0.00020.0002 apart, swap places. At this operating point, then, untuned values do not produce the reordering Efe et al. (2021a) report; the protocol tunes every pipeline regardless, since whether the starting values are adequate cannot be known before the sweep is run.

The estimator matters through its threshold

The estimator axis is swept for ORB and SIFT, one binary and one floating-point descriptor. With the detector fixed, the estimator matters less than the threshold it runs at (Fig. 1): with SIFT every estimator but RHO reaches an mAA of 0.9830.983 to 0.9840.984 at its best threshold, and MAGSAC++ and LMEDS move by less than 0.00010.0001 over the whole range of θ\theta for both detectors, since neither commits to one threshold. The inlier ratio records the threshold rather than the estimate: for ORB it rises from about 0.170.17 to 0.810.81 between θ=0.5 px\theta=$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$ and 4 px4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} whether mAA rises, falls or stays constant.

The ranking at the operating point

Table 4 reports the detector axis on the 2020 evaluation scenes at the selected values. AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK form the leading tie set under all three masking strategies: AKAZE scores highest, at 0.98390.9839 unmasked and 0.98450.9845 under either mask, and the other three lie within the equivalence margin of it (file detectors_comparisons.csv). DISK with LightGlue and ORB follow at 0.9720.972 and 0.9700.970 unmasked, 0.0120.012 and 0.0140.014 behind with intervals clear of zero, and DeDoDe with LightGlue, XFeat and KeyNet with LightGlue trail by 0.0220.022 to 0.0660.066. In pixels the spread at the top is small: with every trial inside the integration interval, mAA over [0,5][0,5] px is one minus the mean CTE divided by 5 px5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, so the margin of 0.010.01 corresponds to 0.05 px0.05\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} of mean error, and the unmasked median error of the tie set lies between 0.075 px0.075\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} and 0.094 px0.094\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}. No pipeline that ran fails on any of the 20002000 trials or leaves the integration interval under any masking strategy. Speed varies far more than accuracy. The unmasked median registration time spans a factor of about thirteen: ORB and XFeat register a frame in 0.10 s to 0.11 s0.10\text{\,}\mathrm{s}0.11\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, SIFT, DISK with LightGlue and RootSIFT in 0.31 s to 0.39 s0.31\text{\,}\mathrm{s}0.39\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, BRISK and AKAZE in 0.50 s to 0.53 s0.50\text{\,}\mathrm{s}0.53\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, and DeDoDe and KeyNet with LightGlue in 0.84 s to 1.3 s0.84\text{\,}\mathrm{s}1.3\text{\,}\mathrm{s}. SIFT reaches the tie set in less than three fifths of AKAZE’s time, and ORB reaches a median error of 0.141 px0.141\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, against 0.075 px0.075\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} for AKAZE, in a fifth of its time.

Deployment regime and rotation

At deployment-scale perturbation every pipeline scores higher, the leading tie set grows from four pipelines to six and no pipeline moves by more than two places. The upright learned models collapse beyond 30 °30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of in-plane rotation (Fig. 2), well outside the 15 °15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of the main configuration. Both sweeps are in Appendix B.

Cost of masking on static scenes

The objects in a static scene move with the ground, so masking them removes correct correspondences or, for a detector that refills its budget, exchanges them for others (Fig. 3), and a small cost is expected. This is the baseline against which the dynamic results of Section 7.5 are attributed to object motion rather than to masking as such. OBB masking costs every pipeline less than the equivalence margin. The largest loss in mAA is 0.00240.0024, for XFeat; for the remaining eight pipelines the change is below 0.00130.0013 in magnitude, and AKAZE, BRISK and KeyNet with LightGlue gain up to 0.00120.0012. HBB masking costs as little: 0.00240.0024 for XFeat and at most 0.00080.0008 for the other eight pipelines, two of which gain. It scores below OBB masking for every pipeline but AKAZE, as the larger mask predicts (a median of 3.56 %3.56\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the frame against 3.32 %3.32\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, Table 3), but by at most 0.00070.0007, so at these object densities the extra area an HBB removes costs almost nothing, and a difference between the two mask shapes in the dynamic benchmark is not explained by the area they remove alone.

7 Part II: dynamic benchmark

7.1 Protocol

Fig. 5 shows the protocol and Table 3 its constants. A case is one hover, the recording of one drone over one intersection cut to its stable part, which lasts two to four minutes (Fonod et al., 2025b), and every sampled frame of it is registered directly onto one reference frame, as the deployed pipeline does. The reference is a frame the case selection picks inside the hover rather than its first: traffic at an intersection comes in phases, and whether a group of vehicles moving together is in view at the reference decides whether capture can occur at all.

Temporal offsets run up to 36003600 frames (2 min2\text{\,}\mathrm{min} at 29.9729.97 frames per second) in twelve bins one octave wide, 11, 22–33, 44–77, 88–1515, and so on to 10241024–20472047 and 20482048–36003600 frames, with 1515 pairs drawn in each bin that holds that many and every offset of the four shortest, 135135 pairs per case, each weighing the same. The spacing follows the mechanism. Capture needs objects present in both frames that moved together, and both conditions decay fast: in the Songdo Traffic trajectories (Fonod et al., 2025c), over all 2020 intersections and 44 days, about 90 %90\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the vehicles in view at a given instant are still in view 4 s4\text{\,}\mathrm{s} later, 64 %64\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} after 16 s16\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, 45 %45\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} after 32 s32\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, 22 %22\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} after 64 s64\text{\,}\mathrm{s} and 5 %5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} after 120 s120\text{\,}\mathrm{s} (lower bounds, since the ends of a hover cut some stays short), and the members of a moving group drift apart within seconds. Evenly spaced offsets would spend most pairs on frames that share no moving group with the reference and average the effect away; the octaves resolve the shortest offsets, where a group is still shared and still moves as one, and the results are read per bin.

Every pipeline of Part I is a candidate, so that a ranking that changes between static and dynamic footage can be observed rather than assumed away, and every candidate runs under all three masking modes on every pair, so masking is a within-pair factor. SIFT, the reference estimator’s own detector, is among them, which makes the one pairing that is circular by construction (Section 4.8) explicit. The candidates run in two regimes, both points of Part I’s budget grid (Fig. 4). The offline regime, for registering a recorded video after the flight, is half resolution with 20002000 features, the operating point of the campaign this work extends (Fonod et al., 2025b). The real-time regime is the grid’s cheapest point, a downsampling ratio of 0.180.18 with 10001000 features, at which six of the ten pipelines estimate a frame’s transform within one frame interval (33.4 ms33.4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}) at the median on the benchmark machine. In both, the inlier threshold is given in pixels of the downsampled frame, so that it keeps its size relative to keypoint localization. The regimes share the cases, the pairs, the reference estimator and the GCP; the mask-margin sweep and the repeated runs are made in the offline regime only. Two further rows are scored on every pair without any pipeline: the identity, which is the unstabilized frame and the transform a failed pipeline delivers, and the reference estimator itself.

Thresholds are tuned again in each regime

The ratio-test and inlier thresholds are not carried over from Part I, where they were selected under synthetic warps of static scenes: moving objects change which correspondences are outliers, and the inlier threshold in particular decides whether matches on a moving group join the consensus. They are tuned in each regime by Part I’s procedure and selection rule, with Part I’s values as the incumbents (a joint grid widened to 1414 ratios from 0.40.4 to 0.990.99 and 1313 inlier thresholds from 0.10.1 to 16 px16\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, selected on mAA, masking disabled), scored against the reference estimator on five tuning cases that the survey selects, one per cell and one control, from the intersections of Part I’s tuning scenes, so that no tuning case shares an intersection with an evaluation case. Offline, SIFT, BRISK and AKAZE move to the strictest corner of the grid, r=0.40r=$0.40$ and θ=0.1 px\theta=$0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$, and XFeat to r=0.45r=$0.45$ and θ=8 px\theta=$8\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$, gaining 0.01020.0102 to 0.01560.0156 mAA on the tuning cases; in real time ORB, AKAZE, XFeat, DISK+LightGlue and DeDoDe+LightGlue move, gaining 0.01000.0100 to 0.12490.1249; the others keep Part I’s values (Tables 1 and 2). The selections at an end of the grid are not followed past it: the offline ones agree with the reference estimator to a median of 0.08 px to 0.20 px0.08\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}0.20\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, and the margin of 0.010.01 mAA corresponds to about 0.05 px0.05\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} of error, both well below the audited floor (Section 4.8), so a stricter setting could only gain agreement with the reference that the audit cannot resolve. The same holds for AKAZE’s θ=0.1 px\theta=$0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$ in real time (0.45 px0.45\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}); ORB’s real-time r=0.99r=$0.99$ lies next to r=1r=1, where the ratio test no longer rejects anything. The thresholds selected without masking are then used under all three masking modes, so a measured masking advantage is not inflated by the tuning.

Cases are selected from the video alone

The hypothesis predicts when capture is severe: where more of the foreground moves, and moves coherently. Testing that needs footage spanning those conditions, so the nine cases are selected by design, on the amount and the coherence of the moving foreground as measured from the video. The candidates come from the hovers of one recording day at the evaluation sites of Part I’s split; the next day in a fixed order is added only if a cell cannot be filled. Every hover is read at points 30 s30\text{\,}\mathrm{s} apart, clear of its first and last seconds and with the full 36003600 frames after them, and each point is a candidate reference frame; a hover supplies at most one case. Each candidate is read the way the benchmark reads it: as pairs of the candidate reference with one later frame in each of the five shortest offset bins (11, 22, 55, 1111 and 2222 frames, the bins’ geometric centers), since every benchmark pair shares the reference and a moving group moves as one only briefly. In each pair the platform’s motion is removed by an affine enhanced correlation coefficient fit to the background (Evangelidis & Psarakis, 2008a), with each frame’s objects filled with the background mean, and every object annotated in the reference frame is sought among the later frame’s detections by appearance: its patch, resampled along its OBB, is compared by ZNCC, and only a mutual best match between boxes of similar size is accepted. A reference object is then found where it was, found displaced (moved by more than a tenth of the median object width), or not found, and the largest set of displaced objects moving together is the largest structure a single wrong homography could fit, both as defined for the capture measure (Section 4.5). Averaged over the offsets, the displaced share of the frame is how many votes the moving foreground can cast, and the share of it moving as one structure, the coherence, is how many it can cast for one model; opposing or crossing streams have low coherence however aligned their boxes are. Distances are measured in object widths, so the procedure does not depend on ground resolution, and nothing is tracked: six annotated frames per candidate suffice. The design is a 2×22\times 2 split at the pool medians (Table 5): a candidate is high moving if its displaced share of the frame is at or above the median and low moving otherwise, and coherent or mixed by its coherence in the same way. Each cell holds two cases, ranked by their margin from the split boundaries, with at most one hover per site in a cell; an unfilled cell is reported, never padded from its neighbor.

The selection reads video alone, which keeps it applicable to footage without trajectories, but the trajectories published for the same recordings (Fonod et al., 2025c) allow its descriptors to be checked. Applying the survey’s definitions to them, in ground coordinates where the platform’s motion is absent by construction, gives an independent value of every descriptor for every candidate (Table 3): the static, moving and coherently moving foreground correlate with their trajectory values at r=0.97r=0.97, coherence at r=0.90r=0.90 and stationarity at r=0.93r=0.93; the two place 81% of the candidates in the same cell and 97% of the quarter farthest from the split boundaries, where the selection draws, and the nine selected cases all fall in the cells the trajectories assign.

The stationary control

A queue at a red light is much foreground with little motion. If masking helps there as much as in a flowing case, the effect comes from removing texture rather than moving objects, and the proposed mechanism does not hold. The design therefore includes a stationary control case, a candidate whose reference foreground mostly stays where it was (the unmoved share of the found foreground in the pool’s top decile, with at least the pool’s median amount of it). Because one case gives one number, the control is also defined at the level of the frame pair: the occupancy persistence between the reference frame’s objects and the current frame’s objects placed in reference coordinates (the intersection over union of the two footprints) is recorded with every measurement, so moving and stationary foreground can be compared within one case, under the same background, which is the comparison the texture confound needs. Table 5 lists the nine cases with the descriptors they were placed on, Fig. 6 shows each at its reference frame, and file offline_masking_scenes.csv characterizes their frames in the terms of Table 3.

7.2 Reference estimator and its audited error

A reference estimator is built from the leading pipelines of Part I under OBB masking (Table 4): AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK cannot be told apart on mAA, and SIFT, the most widely used of the four, is taken. It runs at full resolution with a feature budget of 20 00020\,000 keypoints, a larger mask margin and a stricter estimator (Table 2), and its ratio-test and inlier thresholds are tuned as every Part I pipeline is, on the static tuning scenes against their known homographies, at these settings. The surface is flat, all 7070 grid points within the equivalence margin of the best, so SIFT’s values, r=0.70r=$0.70$ and θ=0.5 px\theta=$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$, are kept, at an mAA of 0.98560.9856 (Table 4). Its homographies 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} are cached once, so every candidate is scored against identical geometry. It runs masked because that is the configuration expected to be most accurate; Section 4.8 states the consequence, which is why the masking result is read primarily off the GCP and the reference-free measures. Choosing the reference on Part I’s ranking assumes what the paper questions elsewhere, that static accuracy transfers to dynamic scenes; it is admissible only because the reference’s accuracy on the dynamic footage is then measured against independent control points rather than inferred.

Ground-plane GCP are annotated in the reference frame and in eight sampled frames per case, two in each of four offset bins (11–33, 44–3131, 3232–511511 and 512512–36003600 frames), the first at the offsets where a moving group is still shared with the reference, and the residual of 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}} against them is reported per offset bin and pooled, with the GCP repeatability beside it.

Over 10641064 points on the 7272 audited frames of the nine cases, the reference estimator’s residual has a median of 0.06 px0.06\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} and a 9595th percentile of 0.38 px0.38\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (2.1 cm2.1\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} on the ground), ranging over the cases from 0.120.12 to 0.65 px0.65\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (Tables 6 and 7). The largest of these is εfloor\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}}, the equivalence margin of every reference-relative pixel metric pooled over the cases, and each case’s own value starts its mAA⁡[εfloor,5]\mathrm{mAA}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}},5]. Per offset bin the 9595th percentile runs from 0.28 px0.28\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at 11–33 frames to 0.53 px0.53\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at 512512–36003600. The GCP repeatability, from the repeat sessions on two cases, is 1.00 px1.00\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at the 9595th percentile, and 61 %61\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the points placed by hand lie within half a pixel of the hidden prediction, the check of Section 4.8 that the clicks did not follow the panel (Table 5 counts how each point was placed). The residual can lie below the repeatability because each later frame’s point is placed by following the reference point’s neighborhood, so the error of the reference click moves the point and 𝐇~k→ref\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}’s prediction alike and drops out; the repeatability is the distance between two unaided clicks of one feature, noise that only the points placed by hand carry. The floor is far below the dilation τ=10 px\tau=$10\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$, so the exclusions placed with the reference still cover the objects. On the audited frames every candidate is also scored against 𝐇GCPk→ref\mathbf{H}^{k\rightarrow\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathrm{GCP}} of Eq. 21, which is the primary geometric evidence for the masking comparison (Figs. 11, 10 and 11).

7.3 Consensus capture

Capture is read four ways: directly, as a capture fraction of at least 0.10.1 on a pair with a moving group (Section 4.5); as an error of many pixels against the GCP where an audited frame falls on such a pair; as error concentrated along the direction of motion; and as all three receding under masking.

Capture by pipeline and case

Without masking, ORB is captured on 2828 of the 304304 pairs that carry a moving group in the real-time regime (9.29.2%), in five cases, and on 66 of them offline (2.02.0%), in two (Figs. 8 and 7; offline in Fig. 1 and file offline_masking_capture.csv). In real time BRISK (66 pairs), SIFT and RootSIFT (22 each) are captured as well, all at offsets below 1616 frames and misaligned by 0.90.9 to 1.6 px1.6\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (CTE50 of the captured), with few of their inliers on the objects found to have moved, a share that undercounts (Section 4.5); offline no other pipeline is. No masked configuration of any pipeline is captured in either regime: the largest capture fraction any masked estimate reaches is 0.050.05 in real time and 0.030.03 offline, below the identity’s 0.070.07, against 6.036.03 and 0.360.36 for unmasked ORB. A higher threshold reduces the count: at λ≥0.25\lambda\geq 0.25 unmasked ORB keeps 1919 captures in real time and 44 offline, at λ≥0.5\lambda\geq 0.5 1111 and none, and at λ≥1\lambda\geq 1 44 and none (released files realtime_masking_capture.csv and offline_masking_capture.csv); it drops partial captures first, so that most of what remains at the top are the breakdowns described below.

Capture follows the survey’s moving-foreground axis. A group of four or more objects that moved together occurs only in the four high-moving cases and, on 1313 pairs, in the stationary control, never in the four low-moving cases, and unmasked ORB is captured in real time in all five cases that have one (released files offline_masking_capture_by_case.csv and realtime_masking_capture_by_case.csv; a case is named here by the hover that ends its name in Table 5): S2 holds 2222 of ORB’s real-time captures and 44 of its offline ones, U1 and F2 two each in real time, B2 and the control one each, and the control the other two offline. The control is still at the survey’s offsets; it holds a group only several seconds after the reference, once part of its standing foreground has started to move together, and its captures lie there. The coherence axis does not order them, since S2 lies in the mixed cell; the survey averages coherence over its offsets, while a capture needs one coherent group at one offset. By offset, 1717 of the 2828 real-time captures of ORB lie within the survey’s offsets of 11 to 3131 frames, 33 of the 44 pairs at one frame among them, and the rest are spread up to the longest bin (Figs. 8 and 2); offline, four of six lie within them. Within the survey’s offsets every capture is a pull toward the group: its error at the group lies within 17 °17\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of the group’s displacement, ORB’s within 11 °11\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} (5 °5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} offline), up to a capture fraction of 0.960.96 (Fig. 1; files realtime_masking_capture_populations.csv and offline_masking_capture_populations.csv), an estimate that registers the group back onto where it stood. Beyond them the real-time captures are of another kind. Apart from one in the control, under a pixel at the group, they are breakdowns: corner errors of 153153 to 7085 px7085\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} on at most 143143 inliers, among them the four at λ≥1\lambda\geq 1, up to 6.036.03. A breakdown is a failure of its own: unmasked real-time ORB’s corner error reaches 100 px100\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} on 4242 of its 12151215 pairs, 2525 of them without a group, and no other configuration’s does in either regime (files realtime_masking_capture.csv and offline_masking_capture.csv).

Examples of captured estimates

Both examples are unmasked ORB on S2. In real time, at an offset of ten frames (Fig. 1), the estimate follows the group almost completely, with a capture fraction of 0.960.96, and its corner error of 10.0 px10.0\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} against the reference is not confined to the group: the error arrows carry the group’s motion across the whole crop, so every position measured in the frame inherits it. Offline, at nine frames (Fig. 9), the pull is partial, a capture fraction of 0.360.36, and the error 4.1 px4.1\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, on 781781 inliers, 12 %12\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} on objects that moved, against 0.8 px0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} on 12791279 inliers under masking. In both the masked estimate has more inliers, because ORB spends the share of its budget the mask frees on the ground (Section 3.2).

Error magnitude

No pipeline fails on any pair in either regime. Against the GCP, every configuration’s median corner error lies between 0.210.21 and 0.57 px0.57\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} offline, below the GCP repeatability, and its 9090th percentile at most 1.15 px1.15\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, reached by unmasked ORB. In real time the medians lie between 0.510.51 and 1.67 px1.67\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}; every configuration but ORB stays within 1.94 px1.94\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at the 9090th percentile, ORB reaches 2.032.03 and 2.07 px2.07\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} with HBB and OBB masks, and 152.57 px152.57\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} without (Tables 10 and 11). That value is set by one frame: the percentile is taken over each case’s eight audited frames and averaged over the cases, and on one audited frame of S2, a pair without a moving group, unmasked ORB’s estimate broke down by 4469.4 px4469.4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (CTEmaxGCP{}^{\mathrm{GCP}}_{\max}). Where a captured estimate falls on an audited frame, the GCP confirm the capture independently of the reference estimator: the four such estimates of unmasked ORB in real time lie a median of 4.3 px4.3\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} from them, where masked ORB’s median is 1.17 px1.17\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, and the one offline 4.7 px4.7\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, against 0.43 px0.43\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} masked (Audited and CTE50GCP{}^{\mathrm{GCP}}_{50} in Table 7 and file offline_masking_capture.csv). The captured SIFT, RootSIFT and BRISK estimates on audited frames lie 1.01.0 to 1.2 px1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} from them, at the repeatability, which cannot resolve a pull of that size. Against the reference estimator, unmasked ORB’s 9090th percentile is 163.44 px163.44\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} in real time (Table 9). For scale, the unstabilized frame lies 6.67 px6.67\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} from the reference at the median (Table 8).

Direction of the error

The identity transform’s motion alignment is 0.4780.478. In real time, unmasked ORB’s is 0.5790.579 against 0.5420.542 under OBB masking, and the planned contrast of AA without masking against OBB masking is 0.0350.035 for ORB, with a 95 %95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} interval of 0.0140.014 to 0.0640.064 and a positive value in five of the six cases where the axis is defined; Holm’s adjustment over the ten pipelines leaves it short of the rule. For the average pipeline it is 0.0050.005 in real time and −0.003-0.003 offline (Fig. 3; files offline_masking_mechanism.csv and realtime_masking_mechanism.csv). AA pools every pair, and capture touches a few percent of them, so it moves little; the capture fraction, which reads the group itself, is the sharper of the two instruments.

Inlier statistics do not reveal capture

Captured estimates are not exposed by their inliers. Pooled over offsets, unmasked ORB’s captured real-time estimates have a median of 290.5290.5 inliers against 504.5504.5 for its other pairs with a group, but inliers fall with offset, and ranked against ORB’s own estimates on the pairs of the same case and offset bin they sit at 0.580.58 in both count and ratio; BRISK’s rank 0.810.81 in count and offline ORB’s 0.930.93 in both (Table 7; file offline_masking_capture.csv). The sharper comparison is with the same case at the nearest offsets, two on either side, whose estimates are neither captured nor broken down. Against those, unmasked ORB’s pulls carry 1.081.08 times the inliers at 1.081.08 times the ratio in real time, and 1.031.03 and 1.041.04 times offline, at a median disagreement from the reference of 9.79.7 and 4.4 px4.4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (18.818.8 and 4.1 px4.1\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} over all captures) where unmasked ORB’s over all pairs is 2.422.42 and 0.54 px0.54\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (Tables 9 and 8): nothing in their inlier statistics sets them apart. The breakdowns carry half (0.510.51 and 0.500.50 times), so theirs do. A captured fit is, by construction, the fit the consensus preferred. Within each pipeline and case the inlier ratio does order estimates by accuracy on the whole: the median Spearman coefficient between ratio and disagreement is −0.38-0.38 without masking in real time and −0.14-0.14 offline, positive in 1616 and 2424 of the 9090 pipeline and case groups (Fig. 10). The pulls are the exception that this ordering cannot reveal. Across pipelines the inlier ratio records the estimator and its threshold rather than accuracy, as in Part I’s estimator sweep (Fig. 1), so choosing a pipeline, which is a comparison between pipelines, cannot rest on it even where it tracks accuracy within one.

7.4 The two regimes

Offline

SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE form the tie set on mAA under every masking mode, led by SIFT with OBB masks at 0.98160.9816 and ending with unmasked RootSIFT at 0.97500.9750; their median disagreements with the reference, 0.080.08 to 0.10 px0.10\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, lie far below the audited floor, and their mAA⁡[εfloor,5]\mathrm{mAA}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{floor}},5] is 0.9980.998 or more. DISK with LightGlue and BRISK follow at about 0.960.96, and every pipeline’s median stays below 0.6 px0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} (Table 8). The GCP separate almost nothing: all thirty configurations are tied against them in corner and center error (Table 10). Three of Part I’s four leaders lead again; BRISK, the fourth, falls level with DISK with LightGlue.

Real time

The same three pipelines form the tie set, from unmasked RootSIFT at 0.88560.8856 to unmasked AKAZE at 0.86730.8673, at median registration times of 1818 to 22 ms22\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}, inside one frame interval. LoFTR follows at 0.8580.858 to 0.8590.859 at 4949 to 57 ms57\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}, then KeyNet and DISK with LightGlue, XFeat, BRISK and DeDoDe with LightGlue between 0.8110.811 and 0.7250.725; masked ORB scores 0.6790.679, unmasked ORB 0.5840.584, and the identity 0.2960.296 (Table 9). Against the GCP every configuration is tied at the median, and at the 9090th percentile all but ORB’s (Table 11). SIFT and RootSIFT share the reference’s detector, which makes their reference-relative scores the least independent of it, so their standing is read against the GCP as well.

7.5 Masking

The primary contrast

For the average pipeline, OBB masking improves every outcome in most cases: in real time ZNCC and GOS in eight of nine, the three outcomes against the GCP in seven; offline the corner error against them in all nine and the others in five or six. No outcome meets the rule of Section 4.9 in either regime, and the primary contrast is not claimed. HBB masks against none read the same way, and OBB against HBB masks differ on no outcome in either regime (Tables 12 and 13). Four of the nine cases never present a moving group, so an average over cases and pipelines dilutes an effect confined to a few pairs of a few cases and of one pipeline.

Masking benefit by pipeline

The gains concentrate in the captured pipeline. In real time, OBB masking improves ORB over its unmasked runs in eight of nine cases on ZNCC, GOS, IoU and OCE against the GCP, by 0.03790.0379 in GOS, with bootstrap intervals that exclude zero; after Holm’s adjustment over the ten pipelines none reaches the rule. SIFT and RootSIFT do not gain: masked, they score lower in ZNCC and GOS in seven of nine cases, by at most 0.00070.0007, and neither change meets the rule. The per-pipeline benefits that meet the rule are small and belong to pipelines that are never captured or only marginally: offline, RootSIFT in GOS and BRISK in ZNCC, by 0.000270.00027 and 0.000090.00009 in all nine cases, and in real time LoFTR under HBB masks in GOS.

Moving objects or the feature budget

Masking can help in two ways. It removes the correspondences on the objects, from which a captured fit is built, and, for a detector that applies the mask before it caps its keypoints (Section 3.2), it hands the removed share of the budget to the ground whether or not the objects moved. The first predicts a benefit concentrated on pairs with a moving group, a captured share that falls under masking, and an error that loses its alignment with the motion. The second predicts a benefit for the detectors that refill their budget, largest at small budgets, that appears in the stationary control and on Part I’s static scenes as well. Both act on ORB, and the two protocols give evidence of each. The budget effect is real: on Part I’s static scenes OBB masking raises ORB’s mAA by 0.0650.065 at the real-time point (Section 6.2), where Part II’s real-time ORB rises from 0.58350.5835 to 0.67850.6785. The captured pairs cannot account for most of that rise. A pair weighs 1/1351/135 of its case and the cases weigh equally, so the 2828 captured pairs can move ORB’s mAA by at most 28/(9×135)=0.02328/(9\times 135)=0.023, and ORB gains in eight of the nine cases although only five ever hold a moving group (Table 13); the rest of the rise is of the size of the budget effect on static scenes. A budget effect cannot make an estimate follow a group, however, and the capture fraction finds that only without masking. The strata agree: in real time the reference-free benefit of the average pipeline is largest in the high-moving mixed cell, which holds S2, and near zero in the low-moving cells and the stationary control (file realtime_masking_benefit_strata.csv). The mechanism contrasts point the same way for ORB in real time, with a positive coverage correlation, a positive persistence gap and a positive alignment contrast, each with an interval above zero and none meeting the rule after Holm’s adjustment. For the average pipeline only the real-time persistence gap in ZNCC has an interval above zero, and offline no contrast points toward capture (files offline_masking_mechanism.csv and realtime_masking_mechanism.csv). In real time the benefit of the average pipeline is positive in every offset bin and both persistence halves, larger for pairs whose foreground moved, and by cell largest in the high-moving cells; offline it is smaller by an order of magnitude and mixed between 1616 and 127127 frames (files offline_masking_benefit_strata.csv and realtime_masking_benefit_strata.csv). With two cases per cell the design reads them descriptively; the within-case contrasts, which match coverage and weigh every case equally, are the test.

Box geometry and mask margin

OBB and HBB masks do not differ on any outcome in either regime. In the offline sweep the masks withhold 2.32.3 to 4.0 %4.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the frame; every geometry and margin gains a few 10−410^{-4} in ZNCC and GOS with intervals that include zero, and OBB at a larger margin do not beat horizontal ones at equal suppressed area (file offline_margin_benefit.csv). Neither mechanism of Section 5 is large enough here to be detected. The survey is flown square to an arterial grid, so most vehicles are aligned with the image axes and their HBB is nearly their OBB: over the frames of the nine cases the HBB cover a median of 2.17 %2.17\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the frame against 2.03 %2.03\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} for the oriented ones (file offline_masking_scenes.csv), so the road an HBB withholds beyond the vehicle, and the shadow it covers beyond an OBB, are both small. At these densities and orientations the suppressed area, not the box geometry, is what a mask changes.

7.6 Behavior with temporal distance

For the average pipeline the disagreement with the reference grows with the offset. In real time it runs from 0.33 px0.33\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} without masking and 0.16 px0.16\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} with OBB masks at one frame to 3.173.17 and 1.09 px1.09\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at 20482048 to 36003600 frames; offline from 0.160.16 and 0.09 px0.09\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} to 0.300.30 and 0.27 px0.27\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, the order of the reference’s own residual (Table 6). Relative to the unmasked median, masking matters most at the shortest offsets, where the captures of Fig. 2 are densest and the masked median is about half the unmasked one in both regimes; in real time the absolute gap peaks where unmasked ORB breaks down, at 6464 to 127127 frames (4.534.53 against 1.09 px1.09\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}) and at the longest offsets (files offline_masking_benefit_strata.csv and realtime_masking_benefit_strata.csv).

8 Discussion

8.1 Interpretation of the capture measurement

Consensus capture is the failure the dynamic protocol was built to measure. In these nine cases it occurs without masking: for ORB at both budgets, in real time in every case that presents a coherently moving group, and by a pixel or two, at the limit of what the GCP resolve, for BRISK, SIFT and RootSIFT at the real-time budget. Under masking it occurs nowhere. This bears on the pipeline with which Fonod et al. (2025b) extracted the Songdo Traffic trajectories (Fonod et al., 2025c), ORB at the offline budget under HBB masks: unmasked, it is captured on 66 pairs, masked on none, which supports masking at detection for trajectory extraction. Three properties make this a measurement rather than an anecdote. The instruments resolve it: a complete capture misaligns the fit where the moving group lies by a sizable fraction of an object width, far above the audited error of the reference and the repeatability of the GCP, and a partial capture still raises the capture fraction and the motion alignment. The cases were chosen to contain it: selected from the video alone, at reference points spread over every hover of a recording day, they span the amount and coherence of moving foreground that pool offers. And the tests were fixed before the outcome: the primary and mechanism contrasts were specified in advance and are reported whatever their result. Capture itself is counted descriptively, at a threshold above what the identity transform reaches, with the counts at stricter thresholds beside it. Of the two descriptors the cases were selected on, the moving share orders where capture occurs and coherence does not: the case with most captures lies in a mixed cell, because the survey averages coherence over its offsets while a capture needs one coherent group at one offset (Section 7.3).

What the cases cannot say is how the effect scales with the moving share. Their moving foreground covers 0.170.17% to 1.941.94% of the frame outside the control (Table 5), and unmasked ORB keeps on average 949949 inliers per pair offline and 513513 in real time in the high-moving coherent cell (released files offline_masking_by_scenario.csv and realtime_masking_by_scenario.csv). The estimator weighs a structure by its share of the correspondences, not of the area (Section 4.1), so the feature budget and the detector’s preference for the high-contrast content of vehicles (Fig. 3) matter as much as the area the vehicles cover, and a low-altitude view over congested lanes, where moving vehicles can fill a large share of the frame, is a different regime. The protocol carries over unchanged; the conclusion need not.

8.2 Joint reading of the two protocols

Part I ranks pipelines against exact truth on static scenes and shows which of their settings matter there: the compute budget, by a wide margin, then the estimator’s threshold for estimators that commit to one, while the matcher thresholds have little effect at the operating point and masking costs almost nothing. Part II asks whether that ranking survives footage in which part of the frame moves. Capture predicts a specific pattern: a pipeline falls without masking, recovers under masking, and has its error along the motion while unmasked, with a capture fraction near one on the pairs that carry a moving group. The data show that pattern for ORB at the real-time budget: its unmasked estimates follow the group with a capture fraction up to 0.960.96 within the survey’s offsets (Fig. 1), and its error along the motion rises; the alignment rises little, since the captures are a few percent of the pairs. Its fall from 0.67850.6785 masked to 0.58350.5835 unmasked is mostly not on the captured pairs, which bound their share of it at 0.0230.023, and the rest is of the size of the budget effect, which masking has on static scenes as well (Section 7.5). For the other pipelines the static ranking carries over: SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE lead Part II in both regimes, masked or not. The static masking cost is the control that makes that reading possible: in Part I the annotated objects satisfy the same homography as the background, so suppressing them cannot improve the consensus, only change which correspondences the budget keeps.

8.3 Practical guidance

No single pipeline is called best. The leading tie set on mAA is AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK under the main Part I configuration and grows to six pipelines at deployment-scale perturbation; beyond 30 °30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of rotation the upright learned models drop out (Fig. 2). In Part II the tie set against the reference is SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE under every masking mode in both regimes; against the GCP every configuration ties at the median in both, and at the 9090th percentile all but ORB in real time (Fig. 11). Offline, masking offers little a practitioner could act on: every configuration lies within the repeatability of the GCP, and the masking benefits are tenths of a pixel or less. In real time it makes ORB usable, at a cost on static scenes of less than 0.0050.005 mAA. For a real-time pipeline the choice is open: masked ORB registers in 1212 to 13 ms13\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} at a median error of 1.171.17 to 1.19 px1.19\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} against the GCP, and SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE, masked or not, in 1818 to 22 ms22\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} at 0.510.51 to 0.57 px0.57\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}; all fit one frame interval at the median, and for the latter three masking changes background alignment by less than 0.0010.001 in either direction, which no contrast resolves (Tables 9, 11 and 13). Compute excludes some pipelines on its own: LoFTR cannot run at Part I’s full resolution on the benchmark GPU, and four of the ten (BRISK, LoFTR, and DeDoDe and KeyNet with LightGlue) need more than one frame interval at the real-time point. HBB and OBB do not differ measurably for registration at these densities and orientations, in the masking contrasts or in the margin sweep; a road grid oblique to the image, larger vehicles at a lower altitude or long turning queues would give the geometry more room to matter, and the protocol measures it there unchanged. OBB remain useful elsewhere, in the motion axis of Section 4.4 and in object-level errors that respect an object’s extent. SIFT and the learned detectors apply the mask after selecting their keypoints in the library evaluated here (Section 3.2), so for them masking can only remove keypoints; selecting after the mask is a change to the library, which the protocol would measure unchanged.

8.4 Limitations

Coverage of the cases

The cases come from one recording day at one altitude band, and their moving foreground at the reference covers at most 1.941.94% of the frame, so what is found about capture holds for that range. Each case is registered onto one reference frame, chosen to span the conditions capture depends on; how often capture occurs over all the frames a deployed pipeline might register onto is a different quantity, which the design does not estimate. Part II has nine independent units at seven intersections: a masking effect is detectable only if it has the same sign in all of them, or in eight with the dissenting case the smallest, and the 2×22\times 2 with two cases per cell is descriptive. Taking the intersection as the unit leaves every claim unchanged, but the per-pipeline benefits that meet the rule fall short of it, since seven units cannot pass Holm’s adjustment over ten pipelines, and ORB’s real-time coverage correlation loses its interval above zero. Cases with a larger moving share, from lower altitudes or congested approaches, and more sites and sessions are the most informative extension; the selection procedure is automated so that they can be added without revisiting the design.

Resolution of the ground control points

The GCP are repeatable to 1.00 px1.00\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at the 9595th percentile. They separate a captured estimate from a correct one and give a masking contrast independent of the reference, but they cannot rank pipelines whose errors differ by less than a pixel, and the reference-relative columns, which can, are limited by the audited residual. With eight audited frames per case, the GCP see only the few captured estimates that fall on one (Section 7.3); the capture fraction, read against the reference on every pair, is what counts them. The reference estimator is a member of the family under test, run with OBB masking; its absolute error is measured by the audit, but not its covariance with a candidate’s, which is why the masking comparison is read from the GCP and the reference-free measures.

Budget, resolution and scene

Part II’s two regimes change the resolution and the feature budget together; Part I separates the two on static scenes (Fig. 4), and the mask-margin sweep was run in the offline regime only. Part I’s 2929 scenes come from one session on one day, so the split prevents tuning on the evaluation scenes but does not make the session representative of other cities, altitudes or lighting. The registration model is a single homography: buildings, raised structures and large tree canopy are excluded from the reference-free measures, but poles, signs and isolated street trees are not, and their parallax grows with the platform’s drift, which within a hover is small and is the same for every candidate. Footage from a translating platform, or with tall structure filling much of the frame, needs a different registration model.

Annotations and object classes

The OBB come from a segmentation-based conversion (Appendix E); its fallback share is zero on this benchmark’s image sets, and where it is not, a comparison between the two box geometries is diluted by it. Most of the benchmark is indifferent to what the objects are, but two parts assume vehicles: the motion axis is recovered from the long axes of OBB, which holds for vehicles and vessels and not for people, and the coherence descriptor assumes a population that moves as streams. Both degrade to an undefined axis and an unfilled cell rather than to a wrong number.

9 Conclusion

Coherently moving objects can capture the geometric consensus of a robust estimator, and the statistics that describe a fit’s self-consistency would then describe the wrong fit. This paper turns that possibility into a measurement for the complete registration pipeline used in reference-frame stabilization of hovering-drone video. A static protocol under exact ground truth establishes what each pipeline can do. A dynamic protocol on nine intersection cases, each registered onto a reference frame selected from the video alone, measures what the same pipelines do when part of the frame moves, at an offline and a real-time budget, with a ground-control-point audit that measures the error of the pseudo-ground-truth reference and scores every candidate independently of it.

On static scenes, four tuned classical pipelines (AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT, BRISK) lead; the compute budget decides accuracy far more than the matcher thresholds, which MAGSAC++ makes nearly irrelevant, and masking costs every pipeline less than 0.0050.005 mAA. On the dynamic cases unmasked ORB is captured in real time in every case that presents a coherently moving group, on 2828 of 304304 real-time pairs and 66 offline, and the estimates pulled toward a group have the inlier statistics of the same pipeline at the nearest offsets. Object masking removes capture for every pipeline at both budgets and restores ORB in real time, though the captured pairs can account for at most a quarter of that gain; it leaves the leading pipelines (SIFT, RootSIFT, AKAZE) unchanged, and HBB and OBB do not differ at these densities and orientations, where the two withhold nearly the same pixels.

How capture scales with the moving share, from lower altitudes or over congested approaches, is the question the benchmark is built to answer next. The protocol needs only annotated boxes for the objects and a dozen or so GCP on each of a handful of frames per case. The benchmark implementation, the data every reported number is computed from, the OBB dataset and the human-verified reference that validates its conversion are released so that the comparison can be extended to other pipelines, other platforms and other classes of moving object without changing the protocol.

It builds on stabilo (Fonod, 2026g) for registration and on hbb2obb (Fonod, 2026e) for object detection and OBB conversion, with the vehicle detector of geo-trax (Fonod, 2026d), whose weights are used under a CC BY 4.0 license.

The data from which every benchmark number in this paper is computed are released under a CC BY 4.0 license (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026b): Part I’s 2929 annotated scenes; Part II’s evaluation and tuning cases with their annotations, GCP and cached reference homographies; the survey output the cases were selected from; and the result directory of every campaign, which records its configuration, package versions and hardware (Appendix A). The CSV files named in the text and table captions are in the record’s supplementary/ directory. Songdo Vision OBB and the human-verified reference that validates the conversion (Appendix E) are a separate record under the same license (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026c).

Appendix A Benchmark protocol parameters

Every campaign is a configuration file in the released implementation, and every result directory records the configuration, its hash, the resolved run grid, the package versions and the hardware it ran on. The implementation was written with the assistance of Claude Code (Anthropic) and is covered by the test suite released with it. The values below are the ones the manuscript’s campaigns use.

Two conventions are worth stating, because a reader comparing against published numbers for the same detectors will otherwise be comparing different quantities. First, the inlier threshold is expressed in pixels of the full-resolution reference frame whatever the processed resolution, which is the convention of the stabilization library: the pipelines estimate current →\to reference, so the reprojection residual is evaluated there, and a threshold quoted in the other frame differs by the scale factor of the transform. Part I’s ranking campaigns and Part II’s reference estimator run at full resolution, where the processed and the full-resolution frame coincide, and Part I’s budget sweep keeps the library’s convention. Part II’s two regimes state the threshold in pixels of the downsampled frame instead, so that Part I’s values, from which their tuning starts, keep their size relative to keypoint localization; 4 px4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} is 8 px8\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} at full resolution in the offline regime and about 22 px22\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} in the real-time one. Because every threshold is tuned at the operating point it is run at, no reported number depends on a rescaling between resolutions. Second, all reported values are for the implementations and versions recorded in each result manifest; as Barath et al. (2023a) document, the same nominal algorithm can differ measurably between libraries, so the implementation is part of what is being compared.

Repeated runs

Jin et al. (2021a) run each evaluation three times and average the results to reduce the randomness in them, which they found negligible. We report single runs instead, having measured how random the estimators used here are. On the OpenCV build recorded in the manifests, homography estimation does not change its output across different global random seeds, at outlier fractions up to 75 %75\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, and does not advance the global random stream either; each estimator seeds an internal generator from a fixed constant. Every method is additionally bit-identical across repeated calls on identical input, with one exception: the parallel LO-RANSAC variant returns one of a small set of matrices depending on thread scheduling, a race that no seed removes. Its spread is at most 1.5×10−31.5\times 10^{-3} px of corner transfer on a 3840×21603840\times 2160 frame, more than two orders of magnitude below the smallest audited resolution floor of Table 6 and therefore not a limitation on any claim made here. For the OpenCV estimators, results are consequently reproducible exactly rather than in distribution. The learned detectors and matchers run under a tensor library whose kernel selection on a GPU is not guaranteed to be bit-exact, so that argument does not extend to them, and the learned pipelines of Part II’s offline regime were repeated three times on one case instead. The repeats agree: every learned pipeline under every masking mode returned the same estimate on all 135135 pairs in all three repeats, and no pair changed between success and failure (released file offline_repeats_repeat_spread.csv).

Appendix B Part I: further results

Table 1 lists the values every pipeline keeps under the rule of Section 4.7 on the 99 tuning scenes at 3030 trials each, over ten ratios rr (0.50.5, 0.60.6, 0.70.7, 0.750.75, 0.80.8, 0.850.85, 0.90.9, 0.930.93, 0.960.96, 0.990.99) and eight inlier thresholds θ\theta (0.250.25, 0.50.5, 11, 1.51.5, 22, 33, 44, 8 px8\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}), with the mAA at the untuned starting values and the number of grid points tied with the best. Where every grid point is tied, no point of the grid is better supported than another, which is why the preset’s values are kept. LoFTR has no row, since it cannot run at the operating point. The other tables behind Section 6.2 are released as files of the data record: the detector axis at the starting values on the evaluation scenes (detectors_default_static.csv) and at deployment-scale perturbation (detectors_hover_static.csv), the rotation sweep of Fig. 2 (rotation_sweep.csv) and the estimator sweep of Fig. 1 (estimators_estimators.csv).

The estimator sweep

The estimator axis is swept for two detectors rather than ten. The estimator sees only the correspondences, and the two cover both descriptor families the classical pipelines use: ORB, the fastest, with a binary descriptor, and SIFT, the reference estimator’s detector, with a floating-point one. Nine estimators at six thresholds already make 108108 runs of 20002000 trials each; all ten detectors would make five times as many, the learned ones among the slowest. With the detector fixed and OBB masking, the estimator matters less than the threshold it runs at (Fig. 1; values in file estimators_estimators.csv). With SIFT, every estimator but RHO reaches an mAA of 0.9830.983 to 0.9840.984 at its best threshold, all within the equivalence margin of one another; RHO peaks at 0.9650.965 and is the only estimator that fails (66 of its 12 00012\,000 trials) or leaves the integration interval (99). With ORB, the three LO-RANSAC configurations, GC-RANSAC and PROSAC reach 0.9720.972 to 0.9730.973 at θ=2 px\theta=$2\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$, MAGSAC++ and LMEDS lie within the margin at 0.9700.970 and 0.9680.968, and plain RANSAC and RHO fall outside it at 0.9400.940 and 0.9250.925. MAGSAC++ and LMEDS move by less than 0.00010.0001 over the whole range of θ\theta for both detectors, since neither commits to one threshold (LMEDS has none), whereas with ORB plain RANSAC loses 0.140.14 and RHO 0.130.13 between their best threshold and θ=0.5 px\theta=$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$. The inlier ratio records the threshold rather than the estimate: at a given θ\theta it is nearly the same for every estimator but RHO, it rises from about 0.170.17 to 0.810.81 for ORB and from 0.770.77 to 0.930.93 for SIFT between θ=0.5 px\theta=$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}$ and 4 px4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} whether mAA rises, falls or stays constant, and the highest inlier ratio in the sweep belongs to neither detector’s best configuration.

The deployment regime

At deployment-scale perturbation (file detectors_hover_static.csv) every pipeline scores higher and the pipelines move closer together: unmasked mAA spans 0.9680.968 to 0.9940.994, against 0.9190.919 to 0.9840.984 in the main configuration. The leading tie set grows from four pipelines to six. AKAZE stays at the top at 0.9940.994, SIFT and RootSIFT follow at 0.9930.993, and DISK with LightGlue, DeDoDe with LightGlue and BRISK lie within the equivalence margin of it, while ORB, KeyNet with LightGlue and XFeat remain outside it. No pipeline moves by more than two places, and no trial fails or leaves the integration interval under any masking strategy. The wider configuration therefore separates the pipelines more than a hovering platform would, without changing which three pipelines lead, which is why the ranking is read from it.

Rotation limits of upright models

Several learning-based detectors do not estimate keypoint orientation, and Fig. 2 (values in file rotation_sweep.csv) shows where that starts to matter. Up to 30 °30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} these pipelines lose accuracy gradually, as the classical ones do: at 30 °30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} XFeat, DISK and DeDoDe with LightGlue score 0.8430.843, 0.8990.899 and 0.9040.904, against 0.9640.964 for SIFT. Beyond it they collapse. XFeat falls to 0.4420.442 at 45 °45\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} and 0.0030.003 at 60 °60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}; DISK and DeDoDe with LightGlue hold 0.8260.826 and 0.8600.860 at 45 °45\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}, fall to 0.1030.103 and 0.4800.480 at 60 °60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}, and reach 0.0000.000 and 0.0760.076 at 90 °90\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}. KeyNet with LightGlue, which estimates orientation, degrades steadily instead, to 0.2240.224 at 90 °90\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}, and SIFT and ORB stay above 0.870.87 over the whole range. The 15 °15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of the main configuration lies well inside the range where no pipeline has collapsed. The limit is a property of the pretrained weights, so it is reported rather than compensated for.

Appendix C Part II: further results

This appendix gives the tables and figures that the main tables of Section 7 summarize. Every one is written by report from the result directories, and the file each caption names holds the rows a table summarizes; the remaining tables are released as files of the data record, written by the same run.

Tuning

Tables 1 and 2 list the thresholds selected in each regime on the five tuning cases, with Part I’s values as the incumbents.

Case selection and the reference estimator

Table 3 checks the survey’s descriptors against the published trajectories, file offline_masking_scenes.csv characterizes the frames of the nine cases, Table 4 reports the tuning of the reference estimator, Table 5 how every GCP of the audited frames was placed, and Table 6 the agreement of the proposals with unaided clicks on two cases.

Capture

Appendix D The analysis plan applied

The rule of Section 4.9 decides what a results table bolds, and the bold is a verdict rather than evidence. The comparisons behind it are released for every bolded column, one row per configuration and outcome: for Part I in file detectors_comparisons.csv and for Part II, one file per regime, in offline_masking_comparisons.csv and realtime_masking_comparisons.csv; the other campaigns’ files are named in their captions. Each row gives the Hodges–Lehmann estimate of the paired difference to the best configuration, its 95 %95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} cluster bootstrap interval, and the exact sign-flip pp adjusted by Holm within the outcome. A reader who disagrees with the equivalence margin can therefore reread every conclusion at a margin of their own, which a table of bolded means alone would not allow.

Appendix E Horizontal-to-oriented box conversion

The OBB are converted from the HBB by hbb2obb (Fonod, 2026e). This appendix summarizes the procedure, selection and accuracy, which Songdo Vision OBB (Fonod & Geroliminis, 2026c) documents in full with the commands that reproduce them.

Procedure

Each HBB, its sides moved outward by a scale factor ss of its width and height (each dimension grows by 2​s2s), prompts one or more SAM-family models (Kirillov et al., 2023a; Ravi et al., 2025a), and an ensemble’s masks are combined by majority vote. The mask is cropped to the scaled prompt and refined by a signed morphological step (Soille, 2004a), its square kernel a set fraction of the shorter side of the largest contour’s bounding rectangle: a positive kernel opens it, removing a thin protrusion such as an overhead sign enclosed by the box, and a negative kernel closes it, rejoining a body split by glare or an occluder. A minimum-area rotated rectangle (Freeman & Shapira, 1975a) is fitted to the largest contour together with any piece holding at least a set fraction of its area. The OBB keeps the class of its HBB; where no valid mask is found, the HBB is emitted unchanged, the fallback whose consequence is stated in Section 5.

Selection

The ensemble, the inference resolution, the prompt scale factor and the signed kernel fraction interact, so they were selected by grid search against the human-verified reference of Section E.1: eleven model configurations, each at 4545 grid points (resolution {896, 1024, 1152}\{896,\,1024,\,1152\}, scale factor {−0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03}\{-0.01,\,0,\,0.01,\,0.02,\,0.03\}, kernel {−0.10, 0,+0.10}\{-0.10,\,0,\,+0.10\}), 495495 conversions of the 5050 reference frames. Mean IoU saturates on tightly fitted boxes: the three leading configurations lie within 0.440.44 standard errors of one another (Tables 1 and 1). Configurations within one standard error of the leader are treated as tied, a heuristic rather than a test, and ties are broken by the share of boxes below IoU 0.750.75 and the 9090th-percentile orientation error, taking the cheapest configuration that leads on both. That is a single sam_l at resolution 10241024, with a scale factor of 0.020.02 and a closing whose kernel is 0.10.1 of that side, at 39 %39\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the inference cost of the leading ensemble.

Accuracy

On the reference, the selected configuration reaches a mean IoU of 0.886 790.886\,79 (standard error 0.001 430.001\,43), a median of 0.917 590.917\,59, 92.1 %92.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of boxes above IoU 0.750.75 and 61.5 %61.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} above 0.900.90, and a 9090th-percentile orientation error of 3.50 °3.50\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}, measured on the frames it was selected on, with exact prompts (Section E.1). With perturbed copies it loses at most 0.0020.002 of mean IoU while the expanded prompt still covers the vehicle, 0.0270.027 under a 2 px2\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} center jitter and 0.0430.043 once the prompt falls short. On the 13451345 vehicles turned off the image axes it raises mean IoU over the HBB itself from 0.60320.6032 to 0.80390.8039 and improves on it for 91.9 %91.9\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of them; over the whole set the 9090th-percentile orientation error falls from 22.69 °22.69\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} to 3.50 °3.50\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}. Segmentation found a usable mask inside all 42454245 reference boxes and all 274 190274\,190 boxes of the release, so neither carries a fallback.

E.1 The human-verified reference

The reference is 42454245 OBB over 5050 frames from six recordings. A detector supplied the HBB; one annotator went over every frame and redrew as OBB the 13451345 vehicles not square to the image, leaving the other 29002900 on their detected geometry, and the set was restricted to the four vehicle classes, rectified to true rectangles, and reconciled one-to-one with the HBB that prompt the conversion, each the exact axis-aligned envelope of its OBB. The unrevised boxes are about 5.8 %5.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} wider across the vehicle than hand-drawn ones, so on the axis-aligned majority mean IoU mixes reference slack with conversion error. An independent DOTA-pretrained oriented detector (YOLO11x-OBB (Jocher & Qiu, 2024a), run tiled and scored class-agnostically), which shares neither architecture nor training data with the conversion, places the axes of these vehicles within a median 0.82 °0.82\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of the reference boxes, the scale against which the conversion’s orientation error is read.
